meta.blurb: Noor has her grandmother's curls and her father's green eyes, and she wants to know why. Her aunt Amara, a scientist, explains the tiny instructions inside every cell, from peas and twins to gene editing, and what they cannot decide.
meta.bible: Noor: an eleven-year-old girl with curly hair and green eyes, curious and quick. Amara: her aunt, Dr Amara, a kind and clear scientist who studies Genes. Grandma: Noor's grandmother, curly hair. They talk through one summer, in the garden and at Amara's laboratory. Key terms: DNA, Gene, Genes, Genome, Cell, Cells, Nucleus, Protein, Proteins, Enzyme, Haemoglobin, Keratin, RNA, Chromosome, Chromosomes, Allele, Alleles, Dominant, Recessive, Mutation, Mutations, Inherited, Heredity, Evolution, Epigenetic, Mitochondria, Neanderthal, Neanderthals, Lactase, Sickle, Malaria, Cystic, Fibrosis, Phenylketonuria, Screening, Counsellor, CRISPR, Eugenics, Twins, Identical, Sequencing, Ancestry, Fingerprint, Epigenetics, Amino, Acid, Acids, Keratin, Dystrophin, Sperm, Embryo, Embryos, Eugenics, Neanderthals, Denisovans, Heritability, Sequencer, Genetic, Genetics, Mosquito, Parasite, Ribosome, Ribosomes, Methyl, Calico, Idris, Jun, Maya, Lina, Okafor. Gregor Mendel: a monk in what is now the Czech Republic who bred pea plants in the 1850s and 1860s; his work was ignored until about 1900. Charles Darwin: English naturalist, On the Origin of Species, 1859. Rosalind Franklin, Francis Crick, James Watson and Maurice Wilkins: the shape of DNA, a double helix, found in 1953; Franklin's X-ray photographs were key. Human Genome Project: ran from 1990 to 2003. Facts: a person has about 20,000 protein-making genes; about three billion DNA letter pairs; 23 pairs of chromosomes; any two people share about 999 in every 1,000 letters; only about 1 or 2 in every 100 letters make proteins; a CRISPR treatment for sickle cell disease was first approved in 2023. Voice: warm, clear, curious; science is real and hedged where it is uncertain; no invented numbers or studies; no real living people named. Idris: Noor's seven-year-old brother, straight dark hair, loves germs and bugs. Mum and Dad: Noor's parents; Mum has curly hair like her own mother, Dad has green eyes. Grandma: Mum's mother, who lives in the house next door, curly hair, tells family stories. Jun: Noor's school friend, who plays football. Maya and Lina: identical twin girls who live on the same street. Dr Okafor: Amara's colleague, a genetic counsellor. The story begins on a Saturday in July and ends on an evening in late August. Noor keeps a Question Book. Biscuit: Grandma's calico cat. This book is general information and is not medical advice.
chapters: More Than a Pea Can Tell

beats.scene: Noor holds up her curly hair beside a framed portrait of her grandmother
beats.summary: Noor has her grandmother's curls and her father's green eyes and asks her aunt why.

beats.scene: Amara arrives at the gate with a suitcase and a white coat
beats.summary: Aunt Amara arrives to stay for the whole summer and promises to answer Noor's question.

beats.scene: Noor and Amara look through an old family album on the sofa
beats.summary: An old photo album shows that curls, green eyes and a gap in the teeth run through the family.

beats.scene: Amara draws a tiny cell on a garden table with coloured chalk
beats.summary: Amara explains that the answer is written in tiny instructions inside every cell.

beats.scene: A glowing blue nucleus sits at the centre of a magnified cell
beats.summary: Most of the instructions are kept inside the cell's nucleus, in a molecule called DNA.

beats.scene: Amara twists a long rope ladder in her hands to show a helix
beats.summary: DNA has the shape of a twisted ladder, called a double helix.

beats.scene: Four coloured letters A, C, G and T float in a glowing line
beats.summary: DNA is written in an alphabet of four letters, A, C, G and T.

beats.scene: A chalk ladder with A joined to T and C joined to G
beats.summary: The rungs always pair A with T and C with G, so each strand matches its partner.

beats.scene: A long thread of DNA is coiled tightly inside a tiny cell
beats.summary: A human cell holds about three billion letter pairs, which would stretch about two metres if pulled straight.

beats.scene: Noor writes her first question on the opening page of a new notebook
beats.summary: Noor starts a Question Book, and Amara says reading one cell's DNA aloud would take nearly a hundred years.

beats.scene: Amara circles a short stretch of the chalk ladder and writes the word gene
beats.summary: A gene is a stretch of DNA that holds the instructions for one product, usually a protein.

beats.scene: Two chalk genes on the table, one tiny and one stretching far across it
beats.summary: Genes come in very different sizes, from a few hundred letters to more than two million.

beats.scene: Amara holds a strand of Noor's hair beside a drawing of a protein
beats.summary: Proteins do most of the work in the body, such as building hair and carrying oxygen.

beats.scene: A single curly hair magnified into a twisted rope of keratin
beats.summary: Hair is made mostly of the protein keratin, and genes help to shape how it grows.

beats.scene: Red blood cells carry tiny parcels of oxygen along a blood vessel
beats.summary: Haemoglobin inside red blood cells carries oxygen from the lungs to the rest of the body.

beats.scene: Noor chews a plain cracker while Amara watches a kitchen clock
beats.summary: An enzyme in saliva turns starch into sugar, so a cracker tastes sweeter the longer you chew it.

beats.scene: A cell copies a gene and sends the copy out to be read
beats.summary: A cell copies a gene into RNA and then uses the copy to build a protein.

beats.scene: A tiny machine reads three-letter words and links coloured beads together
beats.summary: The cell reads the RNA three letters at a time and adds one building block, called an amino acid, for each three-letter word.

beats.scene: A long chain of beads folds up into a neat twisted shape
beats.summary: The chain of amino acids folds into a shape, and the shape decides what the protein can do.

beats.scene: Noor draws a cookbook, a copied page and a finished cake
beats.summary: Noor sums up the chain: a gene is a recipe, the RNA is the copy, and the protein is the dish.

beats.scene: DNA threads wind around tiny spools and coil into a short, thick rod
beats.summary: DNA winds around proteins like thread on spools and then coils into compact bundles.

beats.scene: Forty-six chromosomes arranged in pairs on a pale blue background
beats.summary: DNA is packed into chromosomes, and humans have 23 pairs.

beats.scene: Noor lines up paper cut-outs of chromosomes in pairs from largest to smallest
beats.summary: Scientists photograph chromosomes and sort them into pairs by size, and Noor tries the puzzle with paper cut-outs.

beats.scene: A mother and father hand one chromosome each to a small child
beats.summary: A child gets one set of 23 chromosomes from each parent.

beats.scene: Twenty-three coins fall onto a table, some showing heads and some tails
beats.summary: Which chromosome of each pair goes into an egg or a sperm is decided by chance, like a coin toss.

beats.scene: Two chromosomes cross over and swap matching pieces like trading cards
beats.summary: Before eggs and sperm are made, paired chromosomes swap matching pieces, which shuffles the genes even more.

beats.scene: Idris counts on his fingers while a huge number grows on the chalkboard
beats.summary: Sorting alone allows more than eight million different mixes in one parent, and crossing over makes the number far bigger.

beats.scene: Noor and Idris stand back to back, comparing their heights and hair
beats.summary: Brothers and sisters get different shuffles of the same parents' DNA, so unless they are identical twins they share about half of the DNA that varies.

beats.scene: Amara holds two playing cards to show two versions of one gene
beats.summary: Each person has two copies of most genes, and the versions are called alleles.

beats.scene: Noor colours a chart, with half her pieces from Mum and half from Dad
beats.summary: Noor colours a chart showing that she is a patchwork of Mum's and Dad's DNA, and that on average she shares a quarter with each grandparent.

beats.scene: A monk in a brown robe tends rows of pea plants in a garden
beats.summary: Gregor Mendel studied pea plants in the 1850s and 1860s to find how traits are passed on.

beats.scene: Seven small cards show seven pairs of pea traits, such as tall and short
beats.summary: Mendel chose seven clear either-or traits, such as tall or short plants and round or wrinkled seeds.

beats.scene: A monk brushes yellow pollen onto a pea flower with a tiny brush
beats.summary: Mendel controlled each cross by hand, moving pollen with a small brush so that he knew every plant's parents.

beats.scene: Tall and short pea plants are crossed, and every seedling that grows is tall
beats.summary: When Mendel crossed tall plants with short plants, every plant in the next generation was tall.

beats.scene: Tall and short pea plants stand side by side with tidy labels
beats.summary: Mendel found that some versions of a trait hide others, which he saw as a pattern of three to one.

beats.scene: Amara holds two cards, a capital T and a small t
beats.summary: Mendel's idea was that each plant carries two copies of a factor, one from each parent, and that one version can hide the other.

beats.scene: Noor tosses two coins at once and counts the heads and the tails
beats.summary: Tossing two coins shows why a three to one pattern appears: four equally likely pairings, and three of them contain the dominant version.

beats.scene: Neat rows of counted pea pods lie on a wooden table
beats.summary: Mendel counted tens of thousands of plants over about eight years, so his patterns could not be put down to chance.

beats.scene: Mendel reads a paper to a small, quiet audience in a plain hall
beats.summary: In 1865 Mendel presented his work to a local science society, but few understood it.

beats.scene: Dusty papers of Mendel's pea results lie forgotten on an old shelf
beats.summary: Mendel's work was ignored in his lifetime and rediscovered around 1900.

beats.scene: Noor looks at her own eyes in a mirror and frowns in thought
beats.summary: Noor learns that most traits, like eye colour, are not as simple as a pea plant's.

beats.scene: A close-up eye with a brown ring and green flecks
beats.summary: Eye colour depends on how much of a brown pigment called melanin is in the iris, and several genes control it.

beats.scene: Grandma, Mum and Noor compare their curls, from loose waves to tight spirals
beats.summary: Hair ranges from straight to tightly curled, so many genes work together and there is no single curl gene.

beats.scene: A row of people of different heights stands against a wall chart
beats.summary: Height is shaped by thousands of small gene differences plus nutrition and health.

beats.scene: A doorframe is covered with pencil marks that show children's heights over the years
beats.summary: People in many countries have grown taller over the last 150 years as food and health improved, which shows that surroundings matter.

beats.scene: Idris, freckled across the nose, beside a chart of one gene
beats.summary: A few traits, such as red hair and freckles, are strongly linked to one gene, MC1R, though other genes and the sun also matter.

beats.scene: A newspaper headline about a gene for something is crossed out with a pencil
beats.summary: Headlines often announce a gene for something, but a gene is only a recipe, and a change in it usually raises or lowers a chance a little.

beats.scene: Noor and Idris try to roll their tongues into a tube while Amara laughs
beats.summary: Tongue rolling was once taught as a simple one-gene trait, but identical twins sometimes differ, so it is not that simple.

beats.scene: A chart has two columns, one headed few genes and one headed many genes
beats.summary: A small number of traits depend mainly on one gene, but most traits depend on many genes plus the environment.

beats.scene: Noor draws a football team of tiny gene players passing a ball between them
beats.summary: Noor sums up the chapter: most traits are made by a team of genes working with the environment.

beats.scene: Twin girls in matching yellow coats wave from the park swings
beats.summary: Noor and Amara meet Maya and Lina, identical twins from the same street, in the park.

beats.scene: A single glowing egg splits into two, and two tiny babies begin to grow
beats.summary: Identical twins begin as one fertilised egg that splits early into two, which happens in about three or four births in a thousand.

beats.scene: Two eggs and two sperm make two babies who are not alike
beats.summary: Non-identical twins come from two separate eggs, so they are like ordinary brothers and sisters who happen to be born together.

beats.scene: A scientist compares two sets of twin portraits on a wide desk
beats.summary: Scientists compare identical and non-identical twins: if identical pairs are more alike, genes must matter for that trait.

beats.scene: Maya and Lina stand back to back beside a measuring chart
beats.summary: For height, identical twins are much more alike than non-identical twins, which shows that genes have a large effect on height.

beats.scene: A napkin shows a round chart cut into slices, and a question mark
beats.summary: Heritability describes differences within a group of people, not how much of one person comes from genes.

beats.scene: Identical twins in different clothes, one holding a book, one a ball
beats.summary: Even identical twins differ in some ways, so genes are never the whole story.

beats.scene: Noor presses an inky thumb onto paper beside the twins' fingerprints
beats.summary: Even identical twins have different fingerprints, because the patterns form partly by chance as the baby grows in the womb.

beats.scene: Two twins sit apart on a bench, one holding a book
beats.summary: When one identical twin has an illness such as type one diabetes, the other twin often does not, so something besides genes must matter.

beats.scene: Maya kicks a ball while Lina paints at an easel nearby
beats.summary: Maya loves football and Lina loves painting, and Noor concludes that genes and surroundings work together and are not rivals.

beats.scene: A cell splits in two while a glowing ladder unzips and copies itself
beats.summary: Before a cell divides, the DNA ladder unzips and each side builds a new partner, giving two identical copies.

beats.scene: A zoomed-in strand of DNA shows one letter swapped for another
beats.summary: A mutation is a change in the DNA's letters, often from a copying mistake.

beats.scene: Three versions of a sentence with a swapped, missing and extra letter
beats.summary: A mutation can swap one letter, delete one or add one, and changes of the last two can scramble everything after them.

beats.scene: Sunlight falls on an arm while tiny repair workers mend a broken DNA strand
beats.summary: Sunlight, chemicals and other things can damage DNA, but cells have repair teams that fix most of the harm.

beats.scene: A calm scientist studies a screen showing many harmless gene changes
beats.summary: Most mutations do nothing, a few cause harm and a very few help.

beats.scene: A recipe card says salt instead of sugar beside a flat cake
beats.summary: A harmful mutation can break an important protein, like writing salt in a recipe where sugar was meant to go.

beats.scene: A mountain village in thin air, with smiling people carrying baskets uphill
beats.summary: A rare mutation can help: some people who live high in the Tibetan mountains carry a gene version that helps them cope with thin air.

beats.scene: A skin cell and an egg cell, each with a glowing spot
beats.summary: A mutation in an ordinary body cell stays in that body, and only a change in an egg or sperm cell can be passed to a child.

beats.scene: A long line of ribbons, each slightly different in colour from the one before
beats.summary: Without mutations everything alive would be a copy of the first cell, because mutations are the source of all new versions of genes.

beats.scene: Grandma smiles, showing a tooth gap, beside a framed portrait of her mother
beats.summary: A family feature, such as a gap in the teeth, began as a mutation in some ancestor and was then passed down through the family.

beats.scene: Idris drinks a glass of milk and ends up with a white moustache
beats.summary: Milk contains a sugar called lactose, which babies digest using an enzyme called lactase.

beats.scene: A row of adults in a market, some holding milk and some holding juice
beats.summary: About two out of every three adults in the world make less lactase than they did as children, which is normal and not an illness.

beats.scene: A farmer pours a glass of milk beside a herd of cattle
beats.summary: In some populations a mutation lets adults digest milk, because it keeps the lactase gene switched on.

beats.scene: Arrows on a map show milk-drinking gene changes arising in different places
beats.summary: Different lactase mutations arose separately in Europe, Africa and the Middle East, among peoples who kept cattle, camels or goats.

beats.scene: A mother and child share milk by a campfire as cattle rest
beats.summary: If a gene version helps people to survive and have children, it becomes more common over many generations, which is called natural selection.

beats.scene: A mosquito rests on a bare arm beside a drawing of a tiny parasite
beats.summary: Malaria is caused by a parasite carried by mosquitoes, and it infects red blood cells.

beats.scene: Round red blood cells flow beside curved sickle-shaped ones under a microscope
beats.summary: In sickle cell disease, a change in the haemoglobin gene makes red blood cells curve into sickles, which can block small blood vessels.

beats.scene: A doctor and child talk calmly beside a chart of red cells
beats.summary: A person with only one copy of the sickle change usually stays healthy and is better protected against severe malaria.

beats.scene: A world map with two shaded regions overlapping across warm places
beats.summary: The sickle change is common in the warm regions where malaria has long been a danger, including parts of Africa, the Mediterranean, the Middle East and India.

beats.scene: Noor writes in her notebook beside drawings of a sickle and milk
beats.summary: Whether a gene change is helpful or harmful depends on the surroundings, and evolution has no plan or goal.

beats.scene: A young man in a long coat watches a coast from a ship
beats.summary: In 1831, aged 22, Charles Darwin sailed as naturalist on HMS Beagle for nearly five years.

beats.scene: Darwin sketches a giant tortoise and small brown birds on a rocky island
beats.summary: On the voyage Darwin noticed that individuals within a species differ, and that animals on different islands differ from each other.

beats.scene: Darwin looks at fancy pigeons in cages in the garden of his house
beats.summary: Back in England, Darwin bred pigeons and studied how breeders shape animals over generations by choosing which ones have young.

beats.scene: Three labels on a blackboard read variation, inheritance and survival
beats.summary: Darwin's idea of natural selection needs three things: individuals vary, traits are inherited, and some individuals leave more offspring than others.

beats.scene: Two scientists write letters by candlelight on opposite sides of the world
beats.summary: Darwin waited about twenty years before publishing, until a younger naturalist, Alfred Russel Wallace, independently reached the same idea.

beats.scene: Darwin sits at a wooden desk with finches and notebooks around him
beats.summary: Darwin explained evolution in 1859, and genes later showed how variation is passed on.

beats.scene: Two puzzle pieces, one marked Darwin and one marked Mendel, click together
beats.summary: In the 1930s and 1940s scientists joined natural selection with genetics: mutation supplies variation, and selection sorts it.

beats.scene: A scientist measures a finch's beak with callipers on a dry island
beats.summary: On a tiny Galápagos island, scientists watched finch beaks change after a drought, because birds with larger beaks could crack the tough seeds that were left.

beats.scene: Pale and dark moths rest on a sooty tree trunk in a smoky town
beats.summary: In smoky industrial England the dark form of the peppered moth became common because it was harder for birds to see, and pale moths returned when the air became cleaner.

beats.scene: Noor draws a huge branching tree with small animals and plants at the tips
beats.summary: All living things descend from common ancestors, so they are all relatives, and shared genes are the evidence.

beats.scene: A crowd of many different people smiles together in a sunny square
beats.summary: Any two people share about 999 of every 1,000 DNA letters, and most variation is within groups.

beats.scene: Footprints lead out of a sunny African landscape, across hills and plains
beats.summary: Humans began in Africa more than 200,000 years ago, and groups that left later carried only part of the variety, so Africa holds the most genetic variety.

beats.scene: Noor compares small squares of skin colour on a chart, from palest to darkest
beats.summary: Skin colour is shaped by a handful of genes that were tuned by sunlight over time, and it says very little about anything else a person is like.

beats.scene: A map with soft colour bands fading into one another
beats.summary: Gene versions change gradually from place to place, with no sharp lines between groups, and people have always moved and mixed.

beats.scene: Cards show chromosome numbers for a fly, human, dog and potato
beats.summary: Different species have different numbers of chromosomes, and the number says nothing about how complex the creature is.

beats.scene: A chimpanzee, a fly and a yeast cell are drawn around a small human
beats.summary: Humans share most of their DNA with chimpanzees, and many genes with flies and yeast.

beats.scene: A glass bottle of fruit flies beside a hand lens
beats.summary: Around 1910 Thomas Hunt Morgan bred fruit flies and found that a white-eyed male passed the trait on in a pattern that showed genes sit on chromosomes.

beats.scene: A Neanderthal woman shapes a stone tool beside a fire
beats.summary: Neanderthals lived in Europe and western Asia, made tools, used fire and cared for each other, and disappeared about 40,000 years ago.

beats.scene: Skull of an ancient human relative sits beside a modern human face
beats.summary: Many people outside Africa carry a little DNA from Neanderthals.

beats.scene: A single finger bone in a small box before a cave
beats.summary: In 2010 DNA from a finger bone found in a Siberian cave revealed a third group, the Denisovans, and some people today carry a little of their DNA.

beats.scene: A young scientist studies a pale substance in a glass dish by lamplight
beats.summary: In 1869 Friedrich Miescher found a new substance in the nuclei of cells, which he called nuclein and which we now call DNA.

beats.scene: Two dishes of bacteria on a bench, one rough and one smooth
beats.summary: In 1944 a team led by Oswald Avery showed that DNA, and not protein, carries inherited instructions, and later experiments backed this up.

beats.scene: A scientist writes matching totals for A and T in columns
beats.summary: In 1950 Erwin Chargaff found that in DNA the amount of A equals the amount of T, and the amount of C equals the amount of G, a vital clue.

beats.scene: Two laboratories, in Cambridge and London, with windows lit at night
beats.summary: Several teams raced to find the shape of DNA, including Watson and Crick in Cambridge, and Wilkins and Franklin in London.

beats.scene: Rosalind Franklin adjusts the dials of an X-ray camera in a London laboratory
beats.summary: Rosalind Franklin, an expert in X-ray methods, took very sharp X-ray pictures of DNA fibres and measured them with great care.

beats.scene: A dark X-shaped pattern of spots on a sheet of film
beats.summary: A famous X-ray picture of DNA from 1952, known as Photo 51, showed a pattern that could only come from a helix, and its spacing gave the dimensions.

beats.scene: A model of the double helix is built from wire and coloured beads
beats.summary: In 1953 scientists worked out the shape of DNA, using X-ray photographs by Rosalind Franklin.

beats.scene: A single journal page with a small drawing of a helix
beats.summary: Watson and Crick's paper of April 1953 was only about a page long, and it ended by noting that the pairing suggests how DNA can be copied.

beats.scene: A small rover with solar wings crosses a rusty red desert on Mars
beats.summary: Franklin died of cancer in 1958 at the age of 37, and today a research prize and a space rover carry her name.

beats.scene: Noor twists wire and coloured beads into a double helix model
beats.summary: Noor builds her own model of DNA from wire and beads, with A joined to T and C joined to G.

beats.scene: Amara in a white coat opens the door to a bright, busy laboratory
beats.summary: Amara takes Noor to her laboratory, where machines read DNA, and the first rule is to wash your hands and touch nothing.

beats.scene: A tall sequencing machine glows while a screen beside it fills with coloured letters
beats.summary: A sequencing machine reads the order of letters in DNA, using chemical tags that light up in different colours.

beats.scene: A book torn into thousands of overlapping scraps is slowly pieced back together
beats.summary: A sequencer reads many short pieces, and a computer joins them by finding where their ends overlap, like putting a shredded book back together.

beats.scene: Flags of many countries stand beside a banner that reads the human genome
beats.summary: The Human Genome Project began in 1990, and teams in several countries joined together to read all of human DNA.

beats.scene: A banner on a laboratory wall celebrates a first draft of the human genome
beats.summary: A first draft of the human genome was announced in 2000, and the project was declared essentially complete in 2003.

beats.scene: A tall stack of money beside a tiny computer chip with a price tag
beats.summary: The first genome cost billions of dollars and took more than ten years, but today a genome can be read for less than a thousand dollars in a few days.

beats.scene: A scale tips between a big pile of guesses and a few genes
beats.summary: Before the project, many scientists expected 100,000 or more genes, but humans have only about 20,000 protein-making genes.

beats.scene: A long bookshelf with a few glowing words among many pale blank pages
beats.summary: Only about 1 or 2 in every 100 letters of DNA make proteins; much of the rest helps control genes.

beats.scene: Tiny jumping figures leap along a long strand of DNA beside an ancient virus
beats.summary: Much of the genome is made of old repeating pieces, called jumping genes, and parts that came from ancient viruses, though many other parts of the non-coding DNA do have jobs.

beats.scene: Scientists fill the last gaps in a long glowing strip of DNA
beats.summary: The first human genome had gaps, which were filled in a complete version published in 2022, and since then scientists have been reading many more genomes to see the variety.

beats.scene: Two cells, one from skin and one from liver, glow with different gene patterns
beats.summary: Every cell has the same DNA but uses different genes, so skin cells and liver cells differ.

beats.scene: A dimmer switch and a row of lamps along a strand of DNA
beats.summary: Switch regions of DNA, together with special proteins, turn genes on and off and set how strongly they are used, like dimmer switches.

beats.scene: One cell grows into a tiny ball, then a baby's outline
beats.summary: A fertilised egg divides into stem cells that can become many kinds of cell, and each kind uses its own pattern of genes.

beats.scene: A fly and a baby drawn side by side with matching stripes
beats.summary: A family of master genes, the Hox genes, tells a growing embryo where to put its head, body and limbs, and flies and humans have related ones.

beats.scene: Tiny chemical tags sit on a strand of DNA like small coloured flags
beats.summary: Chemical tags on DNA can switch genes on and off, and they can change with life events.

beats.scene: A calico cat with orange and black patches sleeps on a sunny garden wall
beats.summary: In female mammals one of the two X chromosomes is switched off at random in each cell, which gives calico cats their patchwork coats.

beats.scene: Two older identical twins compare maps of chemical tags on two long scrolls
beats.summary: Identical twins have very similar chemical tags when young, but their tags drift apart as they get older and live different lives.

beats.scene: A long queue of people with empty baskets waits in a snowy street
beats.summary: People who were in the womb during the Dutch famine of 1944 and 1945 showed, decades later, small differences in health and in some chemical tags.

beats.scene: A larger queen bee stands among smaller worker bees on honeycomb
beats.summary: A queen bee and a worker bee have the same genes, but the queen is fed a special food, and this changes which genes are used.

beats.scene: A signpost has one arm marked known and another marked still unknown
beats.summary: Scientists agree that chemical tags matter for how genes work, but the idea that a parent's life experiences change a child's genes in humans is not proven.

beats.scene: A cell cut open shows bean-shaped power plants glowing among other parts
beats.summary: Mitochondria are tiny parts of the cell that turn food and oxygen into usable energy, and most cells hold hundreds of them.

beats.scene: A big cell swallows a small bacterium that stays inside as a friend
beats.summary: Mitochondria probably began as free-living bacteria that were swallowed by a larger cell over a billion years ago and stayed as partners, which is why they have their own DNA.

beats.scene: A mother and daughter at a table with a drawing of a cell
beats.summary: Mitochondria, the cell's power plants, carry a little DNA that is passed on only by the mother.

beats.scene: Grandma, Mum and Noor stand in a row, and a thin line joins them
beats.summary: Noor's mitochondrial DNA came from her mother, who got it from Grandma, and Idris has it too, but he will not pass it on.

beats.scene: A long chain of women hold hands and stretch away into a misty past
beats.summary: Tracing mitochondrial DNA back suggests that all living people descend in the female line from a woman who lived in Africa roughly 150,000 to 200,000 years ago, though she was not the only woman alive.

beats.scene: A father and son hold a certificate that shows the same family name
beats.summary: The Y chromosome is passed from father to son, much as a surname often is, so it can link men who share a distant male ancestor.

beats.scene: Scientists in white suits kneel in a car park around an old grave
beats.summary: In 2012 a skeleton found under a car park in Leicester was identified as King Richard III, partly by matching its mitochondrial DNA to living relatives in his sister's female line.

beats.scene: Noor draws a family tree doubling on a long paper roll
beats.summary: Each person has two parents, four grandparents and eight great-grandparents, and after about thirty generations the number of slots passes a billion, which is more than the people who lived then, so ancestors must appear many times.

beats.scene: A rope is woven from many coloured threads, and some threads end partway along
beats.summary: You inherit only pieces of DNA from distant ancestors, so after many generations you may carry none from some of them, though they are still your ancestors.

beats.scene: Grandma tells a story by lamplight while Noor and Amara listen
beats.summary: Grandma tells the story of how her own grandmother travelled to a new country, and Noor sees that family stories and DNA are two ways of keeping history.

beats.scene: A boy and a girl run across a field while a doctor watches
beats.summary: Some conditions, such as cystic fibrosis, are caused by a change in a single gene.

beats.scene: A tiny gate in a cell wall beside a sticky lung tube
beats.summary: In cystic fibrosis the CFTR gene makes a faulty protein, a channel for salt and water, so the mucus in the lungs becomes thick and sticky.

beats.scene: A man and woman each hold one blue and one red card
beats.summary: A carrier has one working and one changed copy and is usually healthy; in some populations about one person in twenty-five carries the cystic fibrosis change.

beats.scene: Noor tosses a coin four times, while a chart beside her shows the chances
beats.summary: When both parents are carriers, each child has a one in four chance of inheriting two changed copies, a two in four chance of being a carrier and a one in four chance of inheriting neither.

beats.scene: A nurse and a smiling child do breathing exercises beside a small inhaler
beats.summary: Cystic fibrosis is managed with daily care, physiotherapy and medicines, and since about 2012 new medicines that help the faulty protein work have improved many lives.

beats.scene: An old painting shows a queen in black sitting among her many grandchildren
beats.summary: Haemophilia, in which blood clots slowly, is carried on the X chromosome, and Queen Victoria passed the change to royal families across Europe.

beats.scene: A boy and his mother point at a simple chart
beats.summary: In a dominant condition, one changed copy is enough, so a child of an affected parent has a one in two chance; achondroplasia, a form of short stature, is an example.

beats.scene: Two parents of average height hold their newborn baby
beats.summary: Many children with achondroplasia are born to parents without it, because the change arose as a new mutation in an egg or a sperm.

beats.scene: A doctor and a family look at a screen showing rows of coloured letters
beats.summary: There are thousands of rare genetic conditions, and although each is rare, together they affect many people, and reading a genome can help to find a cause.

beats.scene: Noor sorts sticky notes into a small pile and a big pile
beats.summary: Illnesses caused by a single gene are the exception, and Noor decides that people are never defined by their conditions.

beats.scene: Hands hold a scale tipping between a gene card and a plate of food
beats.summary: Common illnesses such as heart disease involve many genes and everyday life together.

beats.scene: Two lines of people face a computer marking tiny differences
beats.summary: Scientists compare the DNA of thousands of people with and without an illness to find the many small differences linked to it.

beats.scene: A tiny weight is added to a large scale
beats.summary: Each of the many gene differences linked to a common illness changes the chance by only a small amount, so a single result tells you very little.

beats.scene: A long ruler with thousands of tiny ticks and a pointer
beats.summary: A polygenic score adds up many small gene differences into one number that can show higher or lower chances, but it is modest in power and has worked best for the groups studied most.

beats.scene: A doctor writes a family health tree on a clipboard while a patient talks
beats.summary: Doctors have long asked about family history, which is a simple and useful clue to inherited chances, though families also share habits and surroundings.

beats.scene: A nurse pricks a newborn baby's heel to collect a drop of blood
beats.summary: Phenylketonuria shows how genes and environment work together: early testing and diet prevent harm.

beats.scene: Two runners at a start line, one with a heavy backpack
beats.summary: A large study found that people at higher genetic risk of heart disease who kept healthy habits had a much lower chance of a heart attack than those who did not.

beats.scene: A doctor explains a chart with one bar higher than another
beats.summary: Some single gene changes, such as certain changes in BRCA genes, raise the chance of some cancers a great deal, but they are not a certainty, and many carriers stay well.

beats.scene: A counsellor in a quiet room explains a chart to a thoughtful couple
beats.summary: A genetic test can show a risk, not a certainty, and counsellors help people understand it.

beats.scene: Dr Okafor sits in a quiet room with a notepad
beats.summary: Dr Okafor describes her work as a genetic counsellor: she listens, explains and helps people decide for themselves, and people have a right not to know.

beats.scene: A person spits into a small tube beside a world map with coloured regions
beats.summary: Ancestry tests compare your DNA to groups of people and give estimates, not exact answers.

beats.scene: A small chip dotted with thousands of tiny spots sits under a bright lamp
beats.summary: A home kit does not read the whole genome but checks hundreds of thousands of chosen spots, and compares them with groups of people in a database.

beats.scene: Two siblings compare two differently coloured pie charts and look surprised
beats.summary: Different companies can give different percentages because they use different databases, and even full siblings can receive different results.

beats.scene: Two strangers meet at a railway station, each holding the same printed chart
beats.summary: Home tests can also find relatives, because people who share long matching stretches of DNA are related, and some families have been reunited this way.

beats.scene: A detective's lens shows a pattern of dark bars from a blood drop
beats.summary: DNA fingerprinting, invented in 1984, helps to solve crimes and prove who is related.

beats.scene: A film strip of dark bars beside repeating letters
beats.summary: DNA profiles count short repeating stretches at about twenty spots, and a match between two unrelated people is extremely unlikely.

beats.scene: A courtroom door opens and a man walks out into the sunshine
beats.summary: DNA profiling was first used in a criminal case in 1986 in England, where it cleared an innocent young man and then helped to catch the real culprit.

beats.scene: A locked wooden box labelled private sits beside a glowing strand of DNA
beats.summary: DNA also tells us about our relatives, so questions of privacy are important: who may keep it, who may see it, and what they may do with it.

beats.scene: A magnifying glass hovers over a coffee cup
beats.summary: DNA at a scene may be there for an innocent reason, and it can be contaminated or mixed, so it is strong evidence but must be handled with care.

beats.scene: Grandma opens an envelope at the kitchen table while Noor watches over her shoulder
beats.summary: Grandma tries a home kit, and the results match her family stories and show a small surprise, which Noor learns to read as an estimate and not a fact.

beats.scene: Jun sits on the garden wall holding a football
beats.summary: Noor's friend Jun asks whether clever people are simply born that way.

beats.scene: A glowing brain with threads joining billions of tiny cells
beats.summary: The brain has tens of billions of nerve cells, built with the help of thousands of genes and then shaped by experience.

beats.scene: A tall pile of thin coloured threads holds up a small bright light bulb
beats.summary: Intelligence test scores are linked to thousands of gene differences that each have a tiny effect, and they explain only part of the differences between people in a group.

beats.scene: Books, a bowl of fruit and a neatly made bed
beats.summary: Schooling, food, reading and sleep all affect how well people think, and average test scores rose over the twentieth century, too fast for genes to be the cause.

beats.scene: One child hides behind a curtain while another waves
beats.summary: Twin studies suggest that genes account for about a third to a half of the differences in personality traits, such as shyness, and the rest comes from experience and chance.

beats.scene: Noor practises scales at Grandma's piano while a small metronome ticks
beats.summary: Noor practises the piano with Grandma and sees that genes may make some things easier, but skill is built by practice.

beats.scene: One child picks a book while another picks up a football
beats.summary: Genes can influence the things a child enjoys and seeks out, and those experiences then shape the child further, so genes and surroundings keep affecting each other.

beats.scene: Two strangers holding matching hats meet in a laboratory
beats.summary: Studies of identical twins who grew up apart have found surprising similarities, but scientists argue about how much to read into them.

beats.scene: A winding path forks into many directions across a green hill
beats.summary: Genes shape possibilities, not destiny; chance and choice matter.

beats.scene: Noor and Jun on the garden wall as Noor writes a list
beats.summary: Noor gives Jun her answer: genes can make some things easier, but they do not decide what you choose, learn, feel or do, and effort matters.

beats.scene: A doctor holds up a card showing a working gene
beats.summary: Gene therapy tries to treat a disease by giving a patient's cells a working copy of a gene that is faulty or missing.

beats.scene: A harmless virus, with its inside emptied, carries a small parcel towards a cell
beats.summary: Gene therapy often uses a virus with its harmful parts removed as a delivery van, which carries the working gene into cells.

beats.scene: A warning sign stands beside a closed door in an old hospital corridor
beats.summary: Early gene therapy trials suffered serious setbacks, including the death of a young volunteer in 1999, and the field became far more careful.

beats.scene: A child reads a storybook in a bright room as a doctor smiles
beats.summary: Gene therapies are now approved for some rare inherited conditions, such as a form of inherited blindness in 2017 and spinal muscular atrophy in 2019.

beats.scene: Bacteria with a gallery of tiny virus portraits in their DNA
beats.summary: Scientists found strange repeating patterns in bacterial DNA, and in 2007 work with yoghurt-making bacteria showed that bacteria use them to defend themselves against viruses.

beats.scene: Glowing scissors are guided to a marked spot on a DNA strand
beats.summary: In 2012 two scientists showed that the bacterial system could be turned into a tool: a guide made of RNA leads a protein called Cas9 to a chosen spot in DNA, where it cuts.

beats.scene: A cursor highlights a single misspelled word in a very long document
beats.summary: CRISPR is like find and replace for DNA, but it can cut in the wrong place, so scientists test it carefully, and newer tools can change single letters.

beats.scene: A patient smiles in a hospital room with a doctor and a blood bag
beats.summary: In 2023 the first CRISPR treatment was approved, for sickle cell disease.

beats.scene: A wheat field with a small tag on each plant
beats.summary: Scientists also edit plants, such as tomatoes and mushrooms, which carries on a very old tradition from farmers to Mendel's peas, though rules differ between countries and people disagree about it.

beats.scene: A price tag with many zeros hangs above a long queue
beats.summary: Gene treatments can cost over a million dollars, and many of the people who could benefit live where such treatment is hard to reach, so fairness is a central question.

beats.scene: A closed laboratory door has a sign and a group of people talking outside
beats.summary: Editing genes in embryos would pass changes to future generations, and many countries restrict it.

beats.scene: A newspaper front page and a crowd of reporters stand outside a hospital
beats.summary: In 2018 a scientist in China announced that babies had been born from edited embryos, and scientists around the world said this was unsafe and wrong, and he was later sent to prison.

beats.scene: A baby in a cot with a list of wishes floating above
beats.summary: Using editing to prevent a serious inherited illness is different from trying to improve traits, and since most traits depend on many genes, designing a baby is not possible and may never be.

beats.scene: A Victorian gentleman with white whiskers writes at a desk in a library
beats.summary: In 1883 Francis Galton, a relative of Darwin, invented the word eugenics for the idea of improving the human race by controlling who has children.

beats.scene: Old black-and-white charts and a closed book lie on a cold desk
beats.summary: Eugenics was a harmful movement that used bad science to judge people's worth.

beats.scene: A wide circle of different faces looks upward under a bright sky
beats.summary: Eugenics was wrong because the science was bad, since most traits depend on many genes and on life, and because no one has the right to judge the worth of another person.

beats.scene: Noor draws a family tree full of curls, green eyes and freckles

beats.scene: Noor adds a new page headed still unknown to the back of her notebook

beats.scene: Amara and Noor sit on garden steps with an open recipe book

beats.summary: Noor ends the summer knowing she is a unique mix, and that this book is general information.
