B1B2: Noor is eleven years old, and her hair curls just like her grandmother's. Her eyes are green like her father's, so she asks her aunt Amara, a scientist, why.
Aunt Amara arrives on a hot Saturday with a suitcase full of books. She is going to stay for the whole summer, and she has promised to answer Noor's question.

In the old photo album, Noor finds curls on Grandma, on Mum and on a great-aunt she has never met. Green eyes look out from Dad's side of the family, and a gap between the front teeth appears in three different pictures.
Amara draws a small round cell on the garden table. She explains that your body is made of tens of trillions of these, and each one holds a copy of your instructions.
The middle of the cell is called the nucleus, and it works like a safe. Inside it is a long molecule called DNA, which holds the instructions.
Amara twists a long rope ladder in her hands until it forms a spiral. This is the shape of DNA, which scientists call a double helix.
Each rung of the ladder is made from two chemical pieces that fit together. We name them with four letters, A, C, G and T, and the order of those letters carries the message.
On the ladder, the letter A always joins with T, and C always joins with G. Because of this rule, each side of the ladder is a perfect partner for the other.
The DNA in a single human cell has about three billion letter pairs. If you could pull it straight, it would be about two metres long.

Noor opens a brand-new notebook, calls it her Question Book and writes the date on the first page. Amara tells her that reading the DNA from one cell aloud, one letter every second, would take almost a hundred years.
A gene is a stretch of DNA that carries one set of instructions, usually for making a protein. A human being has about twenty thousand of these protein-making genes.
Genes come in very different sizes, and Amara draws a short one and a long one on the table. The longest known human gene, which helps to build muscle, has more than two million letters.
Proteins are the little workers that keep your whole body running every day. One called keratin builds hair, and another called haemoglobin carries oxygen in your blood.
Each of Noor's hairs is a thin rope made mostly of keratin. Its shape depends on the little pocket in the skin where it grows, and genes help to decide that shape.
Red blood cells are packed with a protein called haemoglobin, which picks up oxygen in the lungs. Each cell carries hundreds of millions of these proteins on its journey around the body.
Amara asks Noor to chew a plain cracker for a whole minute without swallowing. It slowly starts to taste sweet, because a protein in her spit is breaking the starch into sugar.
When a cell needs a protein, it first makes a short copy of the gene, called RNA. The copy leaves the nucleus, and the cell reads it to build the protein.
The tiny machine reads the RNA three letters at a time. Each group of three letters tells it which small building block, called an amino acid, to add next.
When the chain of beads is finished, it folds itself into a special three-dimensional shape. The shape decides the job, so a protein that is folded wrongly may not work.
In her Question Book, Noor draws a recipe book, a photocopy of one recipe and a finished cake. The gene is the recipe, the RNA is the copy, and the protein is the cake.
To fit inside a cell, DNA winds around tiny spools made of protein. The wound thread then coils again and again until it makes a short, thick bundle.
Your DNA is not kept as one single long thread but cut into pieces. There are 46 bundles called chromosomes, which come in 23 pairs.
Amara gives Noor a sheet of paper chromosomes to cut out and match. Noor sorts them into pairs from the largest to the smallest and finds that she has twenty-three pairs.
Each parent passes on one chromosome from every pair, so you receive 23 from your mother and 23 from your father. That is why you look a little like both of them.
An egg or a sperm does not get both chromosomes of a pair, but only one of them. Chance decides which one, rather like tossing a coin for each of the twenty-three pairs.
There is even more shuffling than that, and it happens before an egg or a sperm is made. The two chromosomes of a pair swap matching pieces, so the new chromosomes are a mixture.
Just by sorting the chromosomes, one person could make more than eight million different kinds of egg or sperm. With the swapping as well, the number is far too big to count.

Noor and Idris have the same mother and father, yet his hair is straight and hers is curly. Each of them received a different shuffle, and they share only about half of the DNA that differs between people.
Because chromosomes come in pairs, you have two copies of most genes. The copies can differ a little, and we call the different versions alleles.
Noor colours a chart with one half for Mum and one half for Dad. Amara explains that, on average, she shares about a quarter of her DNA with each grandparent.
In the 1850s and 1860s, a monk named Gregor Mendel grew thousands of pea plants in his monastery garden. He wanted to learn how traits pass from one generation to the next.
Mendel picked seven clear traits that come in two kinds, such as tall or short plants and round or wrinkled seeds. Peas grow fast and are easy to breed, so he could test many plants.
Mendel did not leave the breeding to the bees. He moved pollen from one flower to another with a small brush, so he always knew exactly which plants were the parents.
First, Mendel crossed tall pea plants with short pea plants, and he waited to see what would grow. To his surprise, every one of the new plants was tall, and none was short or in between.
When Mendel crossed tall pea plants with short ones, all the new plants were tall. In the next generation the short plants returned, about one for every three tall ones.
Mendel guessed that each plant has two copies of every trait, one from each parent. When the copies differ, one version, called dominant, can hide the other, called recessive.
Noor tosses two coins many times and counts how they land, and there are four possible ways. Three of those ways include a head, just as Mendel found three tall plants for every short one.
Mendel grew and counted tens of thousands of pea plants over about eight years. With so many plants, he could be sure that his patterns were not just luck.
In early 1865, Mendel described his experiments to a small science society in the city of Brno. A few people listened politely, but nobody understood how important his work was.
Mendel published his results in 1866, but hardly anyone understood their importance. Around 1900, several scientists found them again, and the science of genetics began.
Noor wonders if green eyes come from a single gene, like Mendel's peas. Amara says no, because several genes work together to decide eye colour.
The coloured part of the eye, the iris, contains a brown pigment called melanin. Brown eyes have a lot of it, blue eyes have very little, and green and hazel eyes fall somewhere in between.
Grandma's curls are tight, Mum's are loose waves, and Noor's lie somewhere in between. Hair comes in every degree of curliness, so many genes must be working together.
Height is shaped by thousands of small differences in DNA, each adding a tiny effect. Food and health in childhood matter too, so genes are only part of the story.
In many countries, people are taller now than their great-grandparents were. Genes did not change in so few generations, so better food and healthier childhoods must have made the difference.
Idris has freckles across his nose, and they grow darker every summer. One gene, called MC1R, has a big effect on freckles and red hair, but other genes and the sun matter as well.

Noor has seen headlines about the gene for happiness or the gene for being good at sport. Amara explains that this is nearly always too simple, because one gene usually changes a chance by only a tiny amount.
For years, textbooks said that rolling your tongue into a tube was decided by one gene. Later studies found that some identical twins differ, which shows that the old story was too simple.
Amara draws a chart with two columns for Noor. A few traits depend mainly on one gene, but most of the things we notice about people depend on many genes together with life.
In her Question Book, Noor draws a football team made of tiny genes passing a ball. She writes that most traits are a team sport, and that the environment is the coach.
One afternoon Noor and Amara meet Maya and Lina, identical twins who live a few doors away. The girls wear the same yellow coats, and Amara can hardly tell them apart.
Identical twins begin when one fertilised egg splits in two very early on. Each half grows into a baby, and this happens in about three or four births in every thousand.
Some twins are not identical at all, because they grow from two different eggs. They share only about half of their varying DNA, like ordinary brothers and sisters, and they can be a boy and a girl.
Scientists compare identical twins with non-identical twins to learn about genes. If the identical pairs are more alike in some trait, the extra likeness must come partly from their genes.
Maya and Lina stand back to back and turn out to be almost exactly the same height. Studies show that identical twins are much closer in height than non-identical twins are.

Scientists say that height is about eighty per cent heritable. This does not mean that eighty per cent of Noor's height comes from genes, because the number describes differences across a whole group.

Even identical twins are not exactly alike, since they have different fingerprints, different experiences and sometimes different health. This shows that your genes and your surroundings work together as a team.
Maya and Lina press their inky thumbs onto a piece of paper, and the two prints are not the same. Fingerprints are shaped partly by chance as a baby grows before it is born.
Sometimes one identical twin gets an illness and the other does not. In type one diabetes, for example, the second twin often stays well, so something besides DNA must play a part.
Maya loves football and Lina loves painting, even though they share almost the same DNA. Noor decides that genes and life are not rivals but partners.
Before a cell divides, its DNA ladder unzips down the middle. Each side then builds a new partner, so there are two complete copies, one for each new cell.
When a cell copies its DNA, it sometimes makes a mistake and swaps one letter for another. A change in the letters like this one is called a mutation.
Amara writes THE CAT SAT and changes one letter to make THE HAT SAT. If a letter is deleted or added instead, every three-letter word after it is thrown out of line.
Copying mistakes are not the only danger, because strong sunlight and some chemicals can damage DNA too. Luckily the cell has repair teams that find and fix most of the harm.
Most mutations have no effect, because they fall in places that do not matter much. A few cause disease, and now and then one turns out to be useful.
Sometimes a changed letter breaks an important protein, and then it cannot do its job. It is like a recipe that says salt where it should say sugar, and the cake does not turn out well.
Now and then, a mutation turns out to be useful. Some people who have lived for generations high in the mountains of Tibet carry a gene version that helps them cope with the thin air.
A change in an ordinary body cell, like a skin cell, stays in that person's body. Only a change in an egg or a sperm cell can be handed down to a child.
Mutations may sound frightening, but they are also the source of all the variety in life. Without them, everything alive would still be an exact copy of the very first cell.
Grandma's gap between her front teeth looks just like her mother's in the old photograph. Amara says that such a feature probably started as a tiny change in one ancestor and then passed down.
Idris drinks a large glass of milk and ends up with a white moustache. Milk contains a sugar called lactose, and babies break it down with an enzyme called lactase.

In fact, about two out of every three adults in the world make much less lactase than they did as children. For them, a big glass of milk can cause stomach ache, and this is quite normal, not an illness.
Most mammals stop making lactase, the protein that digests milk, after they are babies. In some human groups with a long history of dairy farming, a mutation keeps the gene working for life.
The mutations that keep the lactase gene switched on did not all begin in one place. Different ones arose separately among herding peoples in Europe, Africa and the Middle East.
If a gene version helps people to survive and have children, more of the next generation will carry it. Over many generations it can become common, and this process is called natural selection.
Malaria is a serious illness that is spread by the bites of certain mosquitoes. A tiny parasite enters the blood and lives inside the red blood cells.

In sickle cell disease, a change in the haemoglobin gene makes red blood cells bend into the shape of a sickle. These stiff curved cells can block small blood vessels, which causes pain and tiredness.
A person who has only one copy of the sickle change usually stays healthy. That person is also better protected against the worst effects of malaria.
On a map, the places where the sickle change is common match the places where malaria is, or was, a danger. These include parts of Africa, the Mediterranean, the Middle East and India.
Noor writes that a gene change is not good or bad by itself. It depends on where the person lives, what they eat and which illnesses are around, and evolution has no plan.
In 1831, Charles Darwin was twenty-two years old when he sailed on a ship called the Beagle. He was the ship's naturalist, and the voyage lasted nearly five years.

On the voyage, Darwin noticed that no two animals of the same kind are exactly alike. He also saw that similar animals on different islands had small differences, as if each island had its own version.
Back home in England, Darwin kept dozens of pigeons in his garden. Breeders had made very different kinds of pigeon in only a few generations by choosing which birds could have chicks.

Darwin's idea rests on three simple facts, and each one can be checked in nature. Individuals of a kind differ from each other, they pass their traits on to their young, and some have more young than others.
Darwin worked quietly on his theory for about twenty years. In 1858 a younger naturalist, Alfred Russel Wallace, wrote to him with almost the same idea, and that pushed Darwin to publish.

In 1859, Charles Darwin published his idea that living things change over many generations through natural selection. He did not know about genes, but genetics later explained how the changes pass on.
In the 1930s and 1940s, scientists joined Darwin's idea with genetics. Mutations create new versions of genes, and natural selection decides which versions become common.

Scientists have studied finches on one tiny Galápagos island for many years. After a severe drought, only seeds with hard shells were left, and birds with larger beaks lived longer and had more chicks.

In the nineteenth century, factory smoke turned many tree trunks in England black. Dark peppered moths were harder for birds to spot, and they became common, but pale moths returned when the air grew cleaner.
Noor draws a huge tree with a tiny animal or plant at the end of every twig. All living things are descended from common ancestors, she writes, so in a faraway way we are all cousins.
Any two people share about 999 out of every 1,000 DNA letters. Most of the small differences are found inside every group of people, not between the groups.

Our species began in Africa more than two hundred thousand years ago, and Africa still holds the most genetic variety of all. When small groups later spread across the world, they carried only part of that variety.
Skin colour depends on a small number of genes that adjusted to the strength of the sun over many generations. It is a tiny part of the DNA, and it tells you nothing about what a person is like.

If you walk across a continent, gene versions change gradually, and there is no sharp line between one kind of person and another. People have always travelled, traded, married and mixed with each other.
Humans have forty-six chromosomes, but a fruit fly has only eight and a dog has seventy-eight. The number says nothing about how clever or complicated a living thing is.
A human and a chimpanzee share well over 98 out of every 100 DNA letters. We even share many genes with fruit flies and yeast, because all life descends from common ancestors.
Fruit flies breed quickly and cost almost nothing to keep, so they are ideal for experiments. Around 1910, Thomas Hunt Morgan noticed a white-eyed fly among thousands of red-eyed ones.
Neanderthals were close relatives of ours who lived in Europe and western Asia. They made tools, used fire and looked after their injured, and they disappeared about forty thousand years ago.
Scientists can now read DNA from very old bones. They found that people whose families come from outside Africa carry about one or two per cent Neanderthal DNA.

In a cave in Siberia, scientists found a tiny finger bone and read its DNA in 2010. It came from a previously unknown group of people, the Denisovans, and some people today carry a little of their DNA.
In 1869, a young Swiss scientist named Friedrich Miescher found a new substance inside the nuclei of cells. He called it nuclein, but nobody knew what it did, and we now call it DNA.

Many scientists believed that proteins must carry the instructions of life, because proteins seemed more complicated. In 1944, a team led by Oswald Avery showed in bacteria that it was DNA that did the job.
In about 1950, a scientist named Erwin Chargaff measured the four letters in DNA from many living things. He found that the amount of A always matched the amount of T, and C always matched G.
By 1951, several teams were racing to find the shape of DNA. Francis Crick and James Watson worked in Cambridge, while Maurice Wilkins and Rosalind Franklin worked in London.
Rosalind Franklin was an expert in using X-rays to study tiny structures. She and her student Raymond Gosling shone beams through thin threads of DNA and recorded the patterns on film.
One of Franklin's best pictures, taken in 1952 and known as Photo 51, shows a dark X made of spots. That pattern meant that DNA is a helix, and the spacing of the spots gave its size.
In 1953, Francis Crick and James Watson built a model of the double helix. They used X-ray pictures taken by Rosalind Franklin, which gave the vital clue.

Watson and Crick's report appeared in a journal in April 1953, and it was only about a page long. Near the end, they quietly mentioned that the pairing of the letters suggested how DNA could be copied.
Rosalind Franklin died of cancer in 1958 at the age of thirty-seven, and her work was not given proper credit for many years. Today prizes and even a space rover carry her name.
That afternoon Noor builds her own model of DNA from two lengths of wire and coloured beads. She matches red beads to blue ones for A and T, and green to yellow for C and G.
On Monday, Amara takes Noor to her laboratory in the city. Noor puts on a white coat that is far too big for her, and she promises to touch nothing without asking.
The machine in the corner is called a sequencer, and it reads the order of the letters in DNA. It uses tags that glow in different colours, and a camera records the colours one after another.
The machine cannot read three billion letters in one go. It reads millions of short pieces, and a computer joins them by finding where the ends overlap, like putting a torn book back together.
In 1990, scientists began the Human Genome Project, and teams in several countries worked together on it. Their aim was to read all three billion letters of human DNA from start to finish.
The project announced a first draft of the human genome in the year 2000. By 2003, it was declared essentially complete, which was earlier than most people had expected.
The first human genome cost billions of dollars and took more than ten years. Today, a laboratory can read a whole genome in a few days for less than a thousand dollars.
Before the project, some scientists guessed that people would have a hundred thousand genes. The real number turned out to be only about twenty thousand, which is not many more than a tiny worm has.
Genes that make proteins are only about one or two per cent of our DNA. Scientists once called the rest junk, but we now know that much of it helps to control the genes.

A large part of our DNA is made of old repeating pieces that scientists call jumping genes, because they can copy themselves into new places. Some other pieces came from ancient viruses that infected our ancestors.
The first reading of the human genome still had gaps in it. In 2022 scientists published a complete version, and now they are reading many more genomes to see all the variety among people.
Nearly every cell in your body has the same DNA, yet a skin cell is very different from a liver cell. The reason is that each cell switches on only the genes it needs.
Next to many genes there are stretches of DNA that work like switches. Special proteins attach to them and turn the gene on, off or up, rather like a dimmer switch on a lamp.
A baby begins as one fertilised egg, which divides again and again. Its cells slowly become different kinds, such as nerve, muscle and skin, each using its own pattern of genes.
A family of master genes, called the Hox genes, tells a growing embryo where to put the head, the body and the limbs. Remarkably, flies and people have related versions of these master genes.

Small chemical tags attached to DNA can turn genes on or off without changing the letters. This field is called epigenetics, and scientists are still discovering how much our lives can affect these tags.
The patches on a calico cat are a good example, because the cells of a female cat switch off one X chromosome at random. So some patches show orange fur, and others show black.
Studies of identical twins show that their chemical tags are very similar when they are young. As they grow older and live different lives, the pattern of their tags drifts further apart.

In the winter of 1944 and 1945, food was very scarce in part of the Netherlands. Decades later, scientists studied people who had been in the womb at the time and found small differences in their health and their chemical tags.
In a beehive, a queen bee and a worker bee start with the same genes. The young queen is fed a special food, and this changes which of her genes are used, so she grows bigger and lives longer.
Scientists agree that chemical tags matter for how genes work. Whether a parent's experiences can change the tags passed on to a child is still being studied, and in humans it is not yet proven.
Inside your cells there are tiny bean-shaped parts called mitochondria. They turn the food you eat and the oxygen you breathe into energy, and a busy cell may contain hundreds of them.

Scientists think that mitochondria were once bacteria that lived on their own, as tiny free-living cells. More than a billion years ago, a larger cell took one inside, and they began to live together as partners.
Mitochondria are tiny parts of the cell that make energy, and they have a little DNA of their own. You inherit it from your mother, because it comes in the egg.
Noor's mitochondria came from Mum, and Mum's came from Grandma. Idris has them too, but only a mother passes them on, so his children will get theirs from his wife.

If you trace everybody's mitochondrial DNA back far enough, the lines meet in one woman who lived in Africa about two hundred thousand years ago. She is often called Mitochondrial Eve, though many other women lived at the same time.
The Y chromosome is passed down from a father to his sons, in the same way that many families pass on a surname. Scientists can use it to link men who share a distant ancestor in the male line.

In 2012, a skeleton was found under a car park in Leicester, in England. Scientists matched its mitochondrial DNA to living relatives of a king's sister, and the bones were named as King Richard the Third.
Noor draws her ancestors and sees the numbers double each time: two, four, eight, sixteen. After thirty generations, the numbers would pass a billion, which is more people than were alive then.

You receive only pieces of DNA from each ancestor, and the pieces get smaller and smaller as the generations go by. After about ten generations, you may carry no DNA at all from some of your ancestors.
That evening Grandma tells the story of her grandmother, who crossed the sea to start a new life. Noor sees that stories and DNA are two different ways to keep a family's history.
Some conditions are caused by a change in just one gene. Cystic fibrosis is an example, and it appears only when a child inherits the changed gene from both parents.
The gene that is changed in cystic fibrosis makes a protein that works like a small gate for salt and water. When the gate does not work, the mucus in the lungs becomes thick and sticky.
A person with one changed copy and one working copy is called a carrier, and is usually healthy. In some populations, about one person in twenty-five carries the cystic fibrosis change.
If both parents are carriers, each child has a one in four chance of getting two changed copies. The chance is the same for every child, just as a coin has no memory of the last toss.
People with cystic fibrosis follow a daily routine of exercises and medicines. Since about 2012, newer medicines that help the faulty protein to work have made life better for many of them.
Haemophilia is a condition in which blood does not clot properly. Queen Victoria of Britain carried a change in a gene on the X chromosome, and she passed it to several royal families across Europe.
In some conditions, one changed copy of a gene is enough to have an effect. One example is achondroplasia, a common form of short stature, and a child of an affected parent has a one in two chance.
Most children with achondroplasia are born to parents who do not have it. The change was a new mutation in an egg or a sperm, which is a reminder that such changes can appear in any family.

Doctors know of thousands of rare illnesses, and many of them are caused by changes in genes. Each one is rare, but together they affect a lot of people, and reading a genome can sometimes find the cause.
Noor sorts her sticky notes into two piles, a small one and a large one. Illnesses from a single gene are the smaller pile, and Noor decides that nobody should be defined by a condition.
Common conditions like heart disease and diabetes are not caused by one gene. Many genes each add a little risk, and food, exercise and many other things matter as well.
Scientists compare the DNA of thousands of people who have a condition with thousands who do not. They look for small differences that turn up more often in one group than in the other.
Each of these gene differences changes the chance of getting an illness by only a small amount. Taken one at a time, a single difference tells you very little about any person.

Scientists can add up thousands of small gene differences into one number, called a polygenic score. It can show a higher or lower chance, but it is modest, and it works best for the groups that were studied most.
Doctors have always asked about illnesses in a patient's family. This is a simple and useful clue, although families also share food, habits and homes, so it does not prove that the cause is genes.
A rare gene change called phenylketonuria stops the body from breaking down part of some foods. Babies are tested soon after birth, and a special diet then keeps them healthy.
A large study looked at people with a higher genetic chance of heart disease. Those who followed healthy habits had a much lower chance of a heart attack than those who did not.
A few gene changes have a large effect on the chance of illness. Certain changes in the BRCA genes raise the chance of some cancers a great deal, but they do not make cancer certain.
A genetic test can show that a person has a higher or lower chance of a condition. It cannot predict the future, so genetic counsellors help people understand what the results do and do not mean.
Dr Okafor tells Noor about her job as a genetic counsellor. She listens, explains the results and helps people make their own choices, and she reminds them that they also have a right not to know.
Ancestry tests compare your DNA with the DNA of other people around the world. The results are only estimates, and they can change as the databases grow.
A home test does not read your whole genome. It checks hundreds of thousands of chosen spots and compares them with the DNA of groups of people in the company's database.

Two companies can give different percentages for the same person, because they use different databases. Even brothers and sisters can get different results, because each of them inherits a different shuffle of DNA.
These tests can also find relatives, because people who share long matching stretches of DNA must be related. Some adopted people have even met their birth families this way.
In 1984, a scientist found that each person has a unique pattern of DNA, like a fingerprint. Police now use this to solve crimes, and families use it to prove who is related.

A DNA profile looks at spots where short stretches of letters are repeated, and people differ in how many repeats they have. With about twenty such spots, a match between two unrelated people is extremely unlikely.
In 1986, in England, DNA was first used to solve a serious crime. It showed that a young man who had confessed was innocent, and it later helped police to find the real culprit.
Your DNA is very personal, and it also tells things about your parents, brothers, sisters and cousins. Because of this, there are strict questions about who may keep it and who may see it.
DNA found at a crime scene shows that a person was there at some point, but not why or when. It can also be mixed with the DNA of other people, so it has to be handled with care.
Grandma decides to try a home kit, and a few weeks later the results arrive. They match many of her family stories, and they also show a small piece from a place she has never heard of.
Noor's friend Jun comes round with a football and joins them in the garden. He asks whether some people are just born clever, because his cousin finds maths very easy.
Your brain is made of tens of billions of nerve cells, and many thousands of genes help to build and run it. After that, everything you see, learn and do changes the way its cells connect.

Studies have linked scores in intelligence tests to thousands of gene differences, each with a tiny effect. Together they explain only a part of the differences between people in a group, and tests measure only some skills.

Good schools, healthy food, enough sleep and plenty of books all help a child's thinking. Average test scores in many countries rose throughout the twentieth century, which was too fast to be caused by changes in genes.
Studies of twins suggest that genes explain about a third to a half of the differences in personality traits, such as shyness. The rest depends on a person's experiences, friends and plain chance.
Noor practises the piano with Grandma every morning, and slowly the tune improves. Some people may find music easier than others, but nobody becomes good without practice.
Genes can nudge a child towards some activities, such as reading or sport. The child then spends more time on them and gets better at them, so genes and surroundings keep pushing each other along.

Some studies of identical twins who were raised in different homes found surprising similarities in their tastes and habits. Scientists still argue about how to read the results, because the twins may have had similar upbringings.
Your genes shape what is possible for you, but they do not fix your future. Your choices, your surroundings and plain luck all help to decide who you become.
Noor writes a list for Jun of things that genes cannot decide. They include how hard you try, what you choose to learn, how kind you are and what you do next.
If a gene is faulty or missing, why not give the body a working copy? That is the idea behind gene therapy, and it is very easy to say and very hard to do.

Viruses are very good at getting their own genes inside the cells of the body. Scientists take a virus, remove its harmful parts and use it as a delivery van to carry a working gene into the right cells.
The early years of gene therapy were not smooth. In 1999, a young volunteer in a trial died, and other trials had serious problems too, so scientists became far more careful.
Today some gene therapies have been approved for rare inherited conditions. They include a treatment for one form of inherited blindness in 2017 and one for a muscle illness in babies in 2019.

In 1987 scientists noticed strange repeating patterns in the DNA of bacteria, but nobody knew what they were for. In 2007, work with yoghurt-making bacteria showed that they are a defence against viruses.
In 2012, two scientists showed that this defence system could be used as a tool. A guide made of RNA leads a protein, called Cas9, to a chosen spot in the DNA, where it makes a cut.

CRISPR works like the find and replace tool in a very long document. It can sometimes cut in the wrong place, so scientists check it carefully, and newer tools can change single letters without cutting both strands.
In 2023, regulators approved the first medicine based on CRISPR. It treats sickle cell disease by editing a patient's own blood cells, and it is meant for people with serious cases.

Scientists use CRISPR to change plants as well, in a few cases to help them resist disease or keep fresh for longer. People have changed plants by breeding for thousands of years, but opinions differ about editing.
Some gene treatments cost more than a million dollars for one patient. Many people who could be helped live in places where such treatment is hard to reach, so fairness is a very big question.
Changing the DNA of an embryo would pass the change on to future generations, so it raises big questions. Most countries do not allow it to be used to start a pregnancy.

In 2018, a scientist in China announced that he had edited the genes of embryos and that babies had been born. Scientists around the world said it was unsafe and wrong, and a court later sent him to prison.

Some people worry that one day parents will be able to design their babies. Preventing an illness is different from choosing hair or height, and most traits depend on thousands of genes, so nobody can design a child.
In 1883, an Englishman named Francis Galton, who was a relative of Charles Darwin, invented the word eugenics. He wanted society to improve the human race by controlling who could have children.

In the early twentieth century, a movement called eugenics said that society should control who has children. It used poor science and led to great harm, including forced sterilisation in many countries.
Eugenics was wrong for two different reasons, and both of them matter. Its science was bad, and nobody has the right to decide that another person's life is worth less.
Noor draws a family tree and marks who has curls, green eyes or freckles. She sees that each trait appears in some people, hides in others and sometimes returns.
On the last page of her Question Book, Noor writes a list of things that nobody knows yet. Amara reads it and says that science is mostly a careful way of finding out what we do not know.
Amara says that DNA is like a book of recipes rather than a blueprint. The same recipes can turn out a little differently depending on the kitchen, the ingredients and the cook.

C1C2: Eleven-year-old Noor had always been told that she had her grandmother's curls and her father's green eyes, and one warm July morning she finally asked how that could possibly be true. Her aunt Amara, who studied genes for a living, laughed with delight and said that it was the best question anyone had asked her all year. They would spend the whole summer on it, she promised, and Noor would end it knowing a great deal about herself.

On the first Saturday of the holidays, Amara arrived at the gate with a battered suitcase, a bag of notebooks and a white laboratory coat folded over her arm. Noor's parents hugged her, little Idris asked whether she had brought any real germs, and Grandma called across the hedge that supper was nearly ready. By the end of the meal it had been settled that the great question of the curls would be investigated properly, in the garden, every single day.

The old album smelled of dust and peppermint, and as Noor turned its stiff pages she began to see her family as a pattern rather than a crowd of strangers in faded clothes. Curls ran down Grandma's side, green eyes appeared again and again on her father's, and a small gap between the front teeth showed up in photographs taken sixty years apart. Amara tapped each smiling face with her pencil and said that a family album is really an early lesson in genetics, because it proves that things are passed down even when it cannot say how.

Amara took a piece of chalk and drew a small round shape on the garden table, then added a smaller circle at its centre. Your body, she said, is built from tens of trillions of cells like this one, and almost every one of them carries a complete copy of the instructions for making you. Nobody wrote those instructions for you alone, she added, because you inherited them, in pieces, from the people who came before.

The small circle, Amara explained, was the nucleus, a kind of protective vault at the heart of the cell where the most precious material is kept. That material is a long, thread-like molecule called DNA, and it carries the instructions that decide how a body is built and how it runs. Without it, a cell would be like a busy workshop with no plans, and no one to tell the workers what to make.

To show Noor what DNA looks like, Amara took a soft rope ladder from the shed and twisted it slowly until it curled into a graceful spiral. Scientists call this shape a double helix, she said, and it is one of the most famous shapes in all of science. Two long strands wind around each other, joined across the middle by rungs, and the whole thing is far too thin to see without a very strong microscope.

Every rung of the ladder is made of two chemical pieces that fit together like a lock and a key, and scientists name the four kinds with the letters A, C, G and T. It is a surprisingly small alphabet, Amara admitted, yet the order in which the letters are arranged carries an astonishing amount of meaning. In the same way that twenty-six letters can write every book in a library, four can write the instructions for a living creature.

Amara chalked a row of letters along one side of the ladder and then filled in the other side, explaining that the partners are fixed by a strict rule: A always links with T, and C always links with G. Knowing one side therefore tells you the other, rather as a left glove tells you exactly what the right glove must look like. Noor decided that this was the neatest piece of design she had ever seen, and she said so, which pleased her aunt enormously.

Amara wrote the number on the table, three billion, and asked Noor to imagine that many letter pairs packed inside every one of her cells. Stretched out in a straight line, she said, the DNA from a single cell would measure about two metres, though the cell itself is far too small to see. It is folded and wound so cleverly that all of it fits inside, which is one of the great feats of tidy packing in nature.

Noor opened a brand-new notebook, wrote Question Book across the cover in her best handwriting and filled the first page with everything she wanted to know. Amara glanced at the list and remarked that if you read out the letters of one cell's DNA at a rate of one every second, without stopping to eat or sleep, you would be reading for nearly a hundred years. Noor underlined her first question twice, because it suddenly seemed rather a large one.

Amara drew a loop around a short section of the chalk ladder and wrote the word gene beside it. A gene, she explained, is a stretch of DNA that holds the instructions for making one particular product, most often a protein, and a person has about twenty thousand genes of this kind. Together they are rather like a vast collection of recipes, each of which tells the body how to make one important thing.

Amara drew a tiny loop of chalk for a short gene and then walked the line of the next one right across the table and off the edge, to make Noor laugh. Genes vary enormously in length, she said, from a few hundred letters to well over two million in the largest human example, which has a part in building muscle. Size, however, tells you very little about importance, because a short gene can matter just as much as a long one.

Proteins, Amara told her, are the workers and the building material of the body, and almost everything that happens inside you depends on one of them. Keratin gives strength to hair and nails, haemoglobin carries oxygen through the blood, and enzymes speed up the chemical reactions that digest your lunch. A gene is therefore not a picture of a trait but a recipe for a protein, and the traits emerge from what those proteins do.

Under Amara's small hand lens, a single hair from Noor's head looked like a tightly twisted rope, and Amara explained that it was made almost entirely of a protein called keratin. Whether a hair grows out straight, wavy or curly depends partly on the shape of the tiny pocket in the skin from which it grows, and several genes help to determine that shape. Curls, in other words, are not painted on the surface but built into the way each hair is made.

Amara pressed two fingers against Noor's wrist and told her to feel the pulse, because every beat was pushing red blood cells around her body, each one packed with a protein called haemoglobin. Haemoglobin picks up oxygen in the lungs and lets it go wherever the muscles and brain need it, and a single red blood cell holds hundreds of millions of these molecules. A small mistake in the gene for this one protein, she added, would turn out to matter a great deal later in the summer.

Amara handed Noor a plain cracker and asked her to chew it slowly for a full minute, which Noor did with great suspicion. To her surprise it began to taste faintly sweet, and her aunt explained that an enzyme in saliva, a protein that speeds up a chemical reaction, was breaking the starch in the cracker down into sugar. Enzymes are working in every part of the body all the time, and each one is built from the instructions in a single gene.

When the cell needs a certain protein, Amara said, it does not take the precious original out of the nucleus, but instead makes a short working copy of the gene in a related molecule called RNA. That copy travels out into the cell, where tiny machines read its letters in groups of three and join together the right building blocks, one after another. In this way a message written in a four-letter alphabet is turned into a chain that folds up into a working protein.

Amara threaded coloured beads onto a string to show how the cell's tiny protein-making machines work, reading the RNA three letters at a time. Each three-letter word calls for one particular building block, called an amino acid, and the machine links them in order like beads on a necklace, using about twenty different kinds altogether. Noor noticed that with only four letters, groups of three gave plenty of different words, and her aunt told her that this was exactly the point.

A chain of beads is not yet a protein, Amara said, and she scrunched up a long paper-clip necklace to show how it folds itself into one particular three-dimensional shape. That shape is everything, since it decides which job the protein can do, much as the shape of a key decides which lock it opens. If a single bead is wrong, the folding can go awry, and a protein that cannot fold properly may be unable to do its work.

That evening Noor drew a picture in her Question Book of a heavy recipe book locked in a library, a photocopy of a single recipe, and a finished cake on a plate. The gene was the recipe, she wrote, the RNA was the photocopy that the cook carries out of the library, and the protein was the cake that appears at the end. Amara read it twice, said it was better than the diagram in her old university textbook, and asked if she might borrow it.

Amara pulled a long length of cotton from her sewing box and wound it around a row of buttons to show how the cell stores its DNA. The thread wraps itself around little spools made of protein, and the wrapped thread is then coiled and folded again and again until it becomes a compact bundle. Without this clever packing, the two metres of DNA in each cell could never fit inside a nucleus that is far narrower than a human hair.

Noor's DNA, her aunt explained, is not kept as a single endless thread but is divided into forty-six separate bundles called chromosomes, each one a tightly wound package of genes. They come in twenty-three pairs, and one of those pairs, the sex chromosomes, usually decides whether a person is female, with two X chromosomes, or male, with an X and a Y. Every pair has a partner, and the two partners carry matching sets of genes.

Amara gave Noor a sheet printed with the photograph of a cell's chromosomes, spread out like a handful of tiny worms, and a pair of scissors. Noor cut them out one by one and matched each with its partner by length and pattern, as scientists have done for decades, until she had a tidy row of twenty-three pairs from the longest to the shortest. It felt like finishing a jigsaw, she said, except that the picture on the lid was her.

Every child, Amara continued, receives exactly one chromosome from each pair from the mother and the other from the father, so that twenty-three come from the egg and twenty-three from the sperm. The two halves meet at the very beginning of a life and form the first cell, which then divides again and again until a whole person has been built. It explains, in the simplest terms, why a child can resemble both parents and yet be identical to neither.

A body cell carries two chromosomes in every pair, but an egg or a sperm cell must carry only one from each, so that the number comes out right when the two meet. Amara scooped up twenty-three coins and let them clatter onto the table to show that chance decides which chromosome of each pair is passed on, heads for one and tails for the other. Noor looked at the scatter of coins and realised that no two scatters would ever be quite alike.

The coin toss was only half of the shuffling, Amara said, because before the eggs or sperm are formed, the two chromosomes in each pair line up and swap matching pieces with one another. It is like two friends trading handfuls of cards, so that neither hand is quite what it was before, and the chromosomes that are passed on are patchworks of the two that a parent inherited. That swapping is called crossing over, and it happens in every egg and every sperm cell that a person ever makes.

Idris wandered over and asked how many different children Mum and Dad could possibly have, and Amara, delighted, worked it out on the chalkboard. Sorting the twenty-three pairs alone allows more than eight million different combinations in each parent, and the swapping of pieces multiplies that number again beyond anything a person could count. Idris announced that he was therefore one in more than a trillion, and for once nobody argued with him.

Noor and Idris stood back to back in the kitchen while Amara measured them with a ruler and compared their hair, his dark and perfectly straight and hers a springy mass of curls. They came from the same two parents, she reminded them, but each child gets a different shuffle of the family's pieces, which means that brothers and sisters share only about half of the genetic differences between people. Idris said that his half was clearly the better half, and Noor threw a tea towel at him.

Since chromosomes come in pairs, Amara said, you carry two copies of nearly every gene, one inherited from each parent. The two copies are often slightly different, and the different versions of a gene are known as alleles, so that one allele for a certain protein might work a little differently from another. Which of the two shows up in your body depends on how they interact, and sometimes it depends on both.

Noor took a fresh page and coloured one half of a circle blue for her mother's DNA and the other half yellow for her father's, then divided each half again for the grandparents on either side. On average, Amara told her, a grandchild shares about a quarter of her DNA with each grandparent, although luck means that the real figure can wobble a little on either side. The chart was nothing like a photograph, Noor said, but she felt sure it was a portrait of her.

Long before anyone had seen a gene, a monk named Gregor Mendel was growing thousands of pea plants in the garden of his monastery in what is now the Czech Republic. Over about eight years in the 1850s and 1860s he crossed plants with different traits, counted every pod and every seed, and wrote down the results with extraordinary care. He was asking a question that people had wondered about for centuries, which was how a trait passes from a parent to its offspring.

Mendel was careful about what he chose to study, and Amara laid out seven small cards to show his seven pairs of traits. Plants could be tall or short, seeds round or wrinkled, pods green or yellow, and so on, with nothing in between to confuse the counting. Peas also grow quickly and are easy to breed on purpose, which meant that he could follow many plants through many generations in the space of a few summers.

Mendel did not leave his experiments to the bees, Amara said, and she mimed the careful movements of a man with a tiny brush and a steady hand. He carried pollen from the flower of one plant to the flower of another and covered the blossoms afterwards, so that he always knew exactly who the parents were. Because his results depended on that knowledge, the patience he showed in the garden was every bit as important as the cleverness he showed later.

The first result, Amara told Noor, was a puzzle that Mendel must have stared at for a long time. He crossed tall plants with short plants, and instead of a family of medium-sized peas he found that every single seedling grew tall, as if the short parent had left no trace at all. A blending of the two, which most people at the time expected, simply did not happen.

When Mendel crossed tall pea plants with short ones, every plant in the next generation grew tall, and the short trait seemed to have vanished. Yet when he let those tall plants breed among themselves, the short plants reappeared in about one case out of four, a ratio that kept turning up in his counts. He concluded that each plant carries two hidden factors for a trait, and that one can overpower the other, which we now call dominant and recessive.

To explain his results, Mendel suggested that every plant carries two factors for each trait, one from each of its parents, and Amara showed the idea with two cards marked with a capital T and a small t. When the two are different, the stronger factor, which we call dominant, hides the weaker one, which we call recessive, though the hidden one is still present and can be passed on to the next generation. Today we know that these factors are genes, and the different versions are alleles.

Amara handed Noor two coins and told her to toss them together a hundred times, counting how often at least one of them came up heads. Each parent plant, carrying one tall and one short factor, passes on either one by chance, so there are four equally likely pairings, and three of the four include a tall factor that hides the short one. Noor's tally came to seventy-four out of a hundred, which her aunt said was close enough to the three-quarters Mendel had predicted to make him smile.

What impressed Amara most about Mendel was not any single flash of genius but the sheer weight of his counting, for he grew and examined tens of thousands of pea plants over about eight years. A pattern seen in ten plants might be an accident, whereas a pattern that appears again and again in thousands is something much harder to dismiss. He wrote down his numbers honestly and let them speak, and that habit of careful, patient, honest counting is still the foundation of good science.

In early 1865 Mendel stood up in front of a small natural history society in the city of Brno and described eight years of work with peas. The listeners were polite and probably puzzled, for his arguments rested on arithmetic and on ideas about heredity that nobody around him was ready to accept. When the paper was printed and sent to libraries across Europe, it met with silence, and for the best part of four decades almost nothing happened.

Mendel published his findings in 1866, but the scientists of the time barely noticed them, and he died in 1884 without ever knowing how important his peas would become. Around the year 1900, several researchers working on similar questions came across his paper and realised that he had been right all along. From that moment, the study of heredity grew rapidly into the science that we now call genetics.

Noor looked at her green eyes in a hand mirror and asked whether a single gene had decided them, as it had for the peas. Amara shook her head and said that real life is rarely so tidy, because eye colour is shaped by several genes working together, and a few of them matter more than the rest. That is why two brown-eyed parents can sometimes have a child with lighter eyes, and why the old rules from school are only the beginning of the story.

Amara pointed out that eye colour is really a question of how much brown pigment, called melanin, sits in the front layer of the iris. Brown eyes are packed with it, while blue eyes have very little and owe their colour to the way light scatters, much as the sky looks blue although the air is not; green and hazel eyes lie in between. Several genes work together to control how much pigment is made and where it is placed, which is why the colours form a spectrum rather than a few neat boxes.

Grandma, Mum and Noor sat in a row on the back step while Amara studied their hair as seriously as if it were a rare manuscript. Grandma's curls were tight and springy, Mum's were soft waves, and Noor's fell somewhere in between, which showed that hair comes in every possible degree of curl and not in a simple choice between two. Researchers have found several genes that affect it, and none of them acts alone, so there is no single gene for curls that anyone can point to.

Height, Amara said, is a perfect example of a trait that no single gene controls, for researchers have found thousands of small differences in DNA that each nudge it up or down by a tiny amount. Tall parents therefore tend to have tall children, yet food, illness and general care in childhood also play a real part, and populations have grown taller in many countries as nutrition has improved. Genes load the dice, in other words, but the environment helps to roll them.

Grandma kept a doorframe in her kitchen covered with pencil marks that recorded the height of every child in the family, and Amara noticed that the marks crept steadily higher with each generation. Over the last century and a half people in many countries have grown noticeably taller, in some places by as much as twenty centimetres, and the genes of a population cannot change that quickly. Better food, cleaner water and fewer childhood illnesses are the most likely explanation, which shows how powerfully surroundings can alter what the genes allow.

Every July Idris grew a fresh crop of freckles across his nose, and he wanted to know whether a gene was to blame. Amara said that one gene, known as MC1R, has an unusually large effect on freckles and red hair, which makes it a rare case where a single gene has a strong say in how someone looks. Even so, she added, many other genes play smaller parts, and it takes sunshine to bring the freckles out, so the full story is still a team effort.

Noor had cut a newspaper article about the gene for adventurousness out of the paper and stuck it into her Question Book, and Amara read it with raised eyebrows. Such headlines, she said, are shorthand for something far less dramatic, because a gene is a recipe for a protein and not a switch for a personality, and one change in it usually nudges the odds only slightly. When you read about the gene for anything, she advised, ask how big the effect really is and how many other things matter too.

Noor and Idris spent a happy five minutes trying to fold their tongues into tubes while Amara kept count and laughed. Textbooks once used tongue rolling as a perfect example of a trait controlled by a single gene, but later studies of twins found pairs with identical DNA in which one could roll and the other could not. It was a useful reminder, she said, that even famous examples get corrected when scientists look again, and that being willing to be corrected is science working properly.

Amara drew a chart with two columns on the back of an envelope and asked Noor to sort everything they had discussed so far. The short column held the few traits and illnesses that depend chiefly on a single gene, while the long column held height, skin, hair, eye colour and nearly everything else. The first column is the one that Mendel studied so well, she said, but the second is the one that describes most of us.

In the evening Noor drew a football team in her Question Book, with each player labelled as a different gene and the ball marked with the word trait. No single player scored the goal alone, she wrote underneath, because height or hair or eye colour comes from the whole team passing and working together, and the environment stands on the touchline shouting instructions. She showed it to Grandma next door, who studied it carefully and said that it was the best explanation of her own family that she had ever seen.

One bright afternoon Noor took her aunt to the park, where they met Maya and Lina, identical twins who lived a few doors away and wore matching yellow coats. Even Noor, who had known them for years, sometimes had to wait for one of them to speak before she could be sure who was who, and Amara confessed that she had no hope at all. It was a perfect opportunity, she said, because twins are among the most useful people in the whole of genetics.

Amara knelt on the grass and explained that identical twins begin as a single fertilised egg, which for reasons nobody fully understands divides into two groups of cells in the first days of life. Each group grows into a separate baby, and because they came from the same egg, they begin with almost exactly the same DNA, a thing that happens in only about three or four births in every thousand. Identical twins are therefore the closest thing that nature offers to a natural copy of a person, although, as Noor was about to discover, no copy is ever perfect.

Not every pair of twins looks alike, Amara pointed out, because some of them grow from two different eggs that happen to be fertilised at the same time. These non-identical twins, also called fraternal twins, are just like ordinary brothers and sisters who share a birthday, so they share only about half of the DNA that varies between people and may be of different sexes. Lina, as it happened, knew a boy at school who was a non-identical twin and who was nothing like his sister.

Here, Amara said, was the clever trick that scientists have used for generations: they gather large numbers of identical twins and non-identical twins and measure the same trait in each pair. Both kinds of twins usually share a home and a family, so if the identical twins turn out to be more alike than the non-identical ones, the extra likeness must come at least partly from their genes. The method has limits, she cautioned, but it has taught us a great deal that could not have been learned any other way.

Amara asked the twins to stand back to back, and the two of them came out almost exactly the same height, within a centimetre, while Noor, standing next to them, was a head shorter. Studies of thousands of twin pairs have found that identical twins are far closer in height than non-identical twins, which confirms that genes have a very large influence on how tall a person becomes. The twins were pleased to be the centre of a scientific demonstration, and Maya wanted to know whether there would be a certificate.

Amara warned Noor about one of the most misunderstood words in genetics, which is heritability. When scientists say that height is about eighty per cent heritable, they mean that in one group of people about eighty per cent of the differences in height are linked to differences in genes. It does not mean that four fifths of any one person is made of genes, and the figure can change when the surroundings change.

Despite sharing nearly the same DNA, identical twins are never perfect copies of each other, and their fingerprints, for instance, are different. Small accidents in the womb, different friends, different illnesses and different choices all push their lives in separate directions. The old argument about whether nature or nurture matters more has therefore faded, because the evidence suggests that the two are woven together all the way through.

Noor borrowed an ink pad from Grandma's desk, and the twins each pressed a thumb onto a sheet of paper next to hers, so that the three prints could be compared under the magnifying glass. The twins' prints were similar in style yet clearly not the same, which Amara said was because fingerprints form partly by chance, depending on pressure and movement in the womb, and not only through the genes. Even a pair of people with matching DNA, in other words, begin their lives with small differences that nobody planned.

Amara told Noor that twins also teach us humility about disease, because when one identical twin develops an illness such as type one diabetes, the other twin often stays perfectly well. If the illness were written entirely in the DNA, both would be sure to fall ill, so some other factor, whether chance, infection or something in the surroundings, must also take part. These stories are not a reason to ignore family history, she added, but they are a good reason not to treat it as destiny.

Before they said goodbye, Noor asked the twins what they liked best, and Maya said football while Lina said painting, which made both of them laugh because everyone always expected them to like the same things. Noor wrote in her notebook that nature and nurture were not two teams competing for the credit, but two partners who had been working on the same project since before the twins were born. It was a lesson, she thought, that applied to every person she knew, including herself, and she resolved to remember it.

Your body makes new cells all the time, Amara said, to grow, to heal and to replace the ones that wear out, and every new cell needs its own complete set of instructions. Before a cell divides, the DNA ladder unzips down the middle like a zip, and each strand acts as a pattern for building a new partner, following the rule that A pairs with T and C with G. The result is two identical ladders, ready to be shared between two daughter cells.

Each time a cell divides, it must copy all three billion letters of its DNA, and although the copying is astonishingly accurate, a few mistakes slip through. A change in the sequence of letters is called a mutation, and it can also be caused by things such as strong sunlight or certain chemicals. If it happens in a cell that makes eggs or sperm, the change can be passed down to a child.

Amara wrote THE CAT SAT ON THE MAT on a scrap of paper and showed Noor what mutations can do to a message made of three-letter words. Swapping a single letter gives THE HAT SAT, which still makes sense, but deleting one letter pushes every later word out of line and turns the rest of the sentence into nonsense. Cells face the same problem, and changes that add or remove letters can be far more damaging than a simple swap.

Copying errors are not the only way DNA gets changed, Amara explained, because strong sunlight, tobacco smoke and some chemicals can all damage it. Every cell is therefore equipped with a team of tiny repair proteins that patrol the DNA, spot the damage and mend it, and without them life would be impossible. That is one good reason to wear a hat and sunscreen on a hot day, so that the repair teams are not overworked.

Most mutations, Amara explained, are quite harmless, for they land in parts of the DNA that do little or in places where a changed letter still builds the same protein. A small number damage an important gene and can lead to illness, and a rarer few happen to give some small advantage. Every one of us carries dozens of brand-new changes that were not present in either of our parents.

Amara pushed a recipe card across the table on which she had written salt in the place where sugar should be, and she asked Noor what the cake would taste like. A harmful mutation is just like that, she said, because it alters one instruction in an important gene and the protein that results either fails to work or works badly. Many inherited illnesses begin in precisely this way, from a tiny change in one place in the long text.

Now and then, Amara continued, a mutation turns out to be an advantage, and she told Noor about the people who have lived for many generations on the high plateau of Tibet, where the air holds much less oxygen. Many of them carry a particular version of a gene that helps their bodies cope with thin air, and it seems to have spread through the population because it helped people there to survive and raise children. Whether a change is good, bad or neutral, she added, often depends entirely on where its owner lives.

Noor asked whether a sunburn mutation in her skin could be passed on to her children, and Amara told her that it could not. Changes in ordinary body cells, which scientists call somatic mutations, stay inside the person who has them, and although they can occasionally build up and lead to illnesses such as cancer, they never reach the next generation. Only a change in an egg or a sperm cell, which are known as the germline, can become part of a child's DNA.

It was easy to think of mutations as nothing but trouble, Amara said, but they are also the raw material of all the variety of life. If DNA were copied perfectly for ever, every living thing would still be an exact copy of the first cell, and there would be no giraffes, no daisies and no people to wonder about it. Mutation is the way in which the old recipes are constantly rewritten, a little at a time, and sometimes the new versions turn out to work better.

Grandma smiled widely at the camera so that the gap between her front teeth showed, and it was exactly like the gap in the old photograph of her own mother. Every inherited feature in a family, Amara said, began at some point as a change in somebody's DNA, a tiny typing error long ago that did no harm and was therefore passed on, one generation after another. It was a strange and rather wonderful idea that a family joke might be thousands of years old.

Idris gulped down a tall glass of milk at lunch and finished with a white moustache, which gave Amara an idea for the afternoon's lesson. Milk contains a sugar called lactose, she said, and every baby mammal makes an enzyme called lactase to break it down, so that the milk can feed it. The gene that makes lactase is a good example of how an ordinary-looking piece of DNA can have a surprisingly interesting history.

Many adults, Amara told her, cannot drink a large glass of milk without feeling unwell, and worldwide it is the majority. About two out of every three adults make much less lactase than they did as small children, and milk can leave them with a sore stomach, though a little yoghurt or cheese is often fine. This is the normal state of affairs for a mammal, so it is not an illness, and it is the people who can drink milk all their lives who are the unusual ones.

Most mammals stop making lactase, the enzyme that digests the sugar in milk, soon after they are weaned, and for most of human history so did people. In several parts of the world where herding and dairy farming were common, however, mutations arose that keep the lactase gene active into adulthood, and they spread because they gave their carriers a useful source of food. It is a clear case of a human population changing in response to its way of life.

Amara drew a map of the Old World and added arrows to show where researchers have found mutations that keep the lactase gene switched on. They did not all start in one place, she said, for different changes arose separately among cattle herders in Europe, among herders of cattle and camels in Africa, and in parts of the Middle East. It is a striking case of the same problem being solved more than once, by chance, in unconnected groups of people.

Why should such a change have spread, Noor wanted to know, and Amara answered with a simple idea. Where fresh milk was an important food, a person who could digest it was likely to be a little better nourished and more likely to raise healthy children, who in turn inherited the useful gene. Repeat that for hundreds of generations and a rare mutation can become common, which is the process called natural selection, and it does not need any plan at all.

To explain the next story, Amara had to tell Noor about malaria, a dangerous illness that is spread from person to person by the bites of certain kinds of mosquito. The cause is a parasite that enters the bloodstream and spends part of its life inside red blood cells, and for thousands of years it has killed many children in warm parts of the world. It also turns out to be one of the strongest forces that have shaped human DNA.

Remember the haemoglobin gene from the first week, Amara said, because a single changed letter in it can bend red blood cells into the shape of a sickle. A person who inherits the changed version from both parents has sickle cell disease, in which the stiff curved cells can block tiny blood vessels, causing pain, tiredness and a risk of serious complications. Doctors can treat the condition in several ways today, and there are ways of managing it that did not exist a generation ago.

Here was the real puzzle, Amara said, because a mutation that causes a serious disease in people with two copies ought to have disappeared long ago. The answer is that a person with only one copy, who is usually healthy, is better protected against the worst effects of malaria, so where the disease is common the change gave its carriers a net advantage. Evolution does not weigh happiness, she added, and it simply counts how many children survive.

Noor looked at the two maps that Amara laid side by side, one showing where the sickle change is common and one showing where malaria has long been a threat, and she saw at once that they matched. Parts of Africa, the countries around the Mediterranean, the Middle East and India all appear on both, and the pattern is exactly what natural selection would predict. It is one of the clearest cases in all of biology of the environment shaping the genes of a whole population.

That evening Noor wrote two examples at the head of a clean page, one about milk and one about malaria, and beneath them she summarised what the two stories meant. A gene change is not good or bad on its own, she wrote, because its effect depends on diet, climate and the diseases that surround it, and evolution has no plan and aims at nothing. Amara read the note and remarked that the last line was the one that most grown-ups still found hard to accept.

In December 1831 a young Englishman named Charles Darwin, who was just twenty-two, boarded a small sailing ship called the Beagle as the expedition's naturalist. The voyage was meant to chart coastlines, but for Darwin it became a five-year education, during which he collected plants, animals and fossils from South America to the Pacific. Noor liked the idea that one of the great thinkers of science began as a young man who was not sure what he wanted to do.

On the Beagle's journey Darwin noticed something that most people take for granted, which is that no two individuals of the same species are exactly alike. On the Galápagos Islands, off the coast of South America, he also saw that tortoises, mockingbirds and small brown birds differed a little from island to island, as if each place had grown its own version. He did not understand the meaning of it at the time, and only later, back in England, did the pieces begin to fit.

Back in England, Darwin took up the strange hobby of keeping fancy pigeons, which came in an astonishing variety of shapes, from puffed-up chests to fan-shaped tails. Breeders had created all of these forms in a few generations simply by choosing which birds should raise chicks, and Darwin realised that he was looking at a small and quick version of something that nature might do slowly. It was the sort of observation that seems obvious only after somebody has made it.

Amara wrote three words on the chalkboard to sum up Darwin's great idea: variation, inheritance and survival. Individuals in a species differ from one another, many of those differences are passed on to their offspring, and since more young are born than can possibly survive, those with helpful traits tend to leave more descendants than the rest. Given enough generations, Darwin argued, the population will change, and no designer is needed to guide it.

Darwin was a cautious man who knew that his idea would cause a storm, so he worked on it quietly for some twenty years. In 1858 he received a letter from a younger naturalist called Alfred Russel Wallace, who was working in Southeast Asia and had independently arrived at almost exactly the same theory. The two men arranged for their ideas to be presented together, and Darwin hurriedly finished the book that he had been preparing for so long.

In 1859, Charles Darwin published On the Origin of Species, arguing that living things change over many generations because individuals with helpful traits tend to leave more offspring. He had no idea how traits were inherited, and Mendel's paper was gathering dust in libraries across Europe. Once genetics was joined with his theory in the twentieth century, mutation and inheritance supplied the missing machinery, and the picture of evolution became far more complete.

The two halves of the puzzle, Amara said, finally came together in the 1930s and 1940s, when scientists combined Darwin's natural selection with Mendel's genetics and the mathematics of populations. Mutation and shuffling provide the variation, inheritance carries it forward, and selection acts on it, which is why a change in the frequency of gene versions in a population is what we now mean by evolution. Noor drew two puzzle pieces in her notebook and wrote their names on them with a satisfied sigh.

Evolution is not only a story from the distant past, Amara said, and she described how scientists have spent decades measuring the finches of one tiny island in the Galápagos. When a severe drought killed off most of the soft seeds, the birds with larger, deeper beaks were better at cracking the hard ones that remained, and they survived and bred more successfully. In the next generation the average beak was measurably bigger, so that natural selection had been caught in the act.

Amara's second example came from the factory towns of Victorian England, where soot from chimneys blackened the trunks of the trees. Dark peppered moths, which had once been rare, blended in against the black bark and escaped the notice of hungry birds, so they became the common form, whereas the pale ones were picked off. After laws cleaned up the air in the twentieth century the pale moths returned, as the environment shifted back and selection followed it.

Noor spread two pages across the garden table and drew a huge branching tree, with a tiny animal, plant or fungus at the tip of every twig and herself, in pencil, on one of the highest branches. All living things descend from common ancestors, she wrote, which means that every creature, from a daisy to a dolphin, is a very distant cousin of every other. Amara looked at the drawing for a long time and said that of all the facts she knew, this was the one that still gave her goosebumps.

Amara told Noor that any two humans, however far apart they live, share about 999 of every thousand letters in their DNA, which makes us an unusually similar species. Of the small amount that does vary, most of the variation is found within any one population rather than between populations, so that two neighbours can differ more than two strangers from opposite sides of the world. The old idea of sharply divided biological races has no real support in the genetic evidence.

Our species first appeared in Africa more than two hundred thousand years ago, and for a long time everyone lived there. When small groups finally set out to settle the rest of the world, tens of thousands of years ago, each carried only a sample of the variety present at home. That is why people in Africa today have more genetic variety than people anywhere else, and in a sense the rest of humanity is one branch of that family tree.

Noor held a chart of skin shades against her own arm and asked why people look so different if their DNA is so similar. Skin colour, Amara explained, depends on a small number of genes tuned by sunlight over many generations, because dark skin guards against strong ultraviolet rays and pale skin makes vitamin D more easily where the sun is weak. It is a tiny and very visible corner of the genome, she said, and it says nothing at all about a person's talents, character or intelligence.

Amara showed Noor a map on which gene versions were shaded in soft colours, and the shades slid into one another gradually, with no hard borders anywhere. Walk across a continent, she said, and the frequencies of different versions change a little at a time, because people have always travelled, traded and married, so there is no point where one kind of human ends and another begins. The boundaries that people draw between groups come from history and customs, not from the DNA.

Amara laid out a few cards on which she had written the chromosome numbers of different species, and Noor laughed at the result. A fruit fly has eight, a human has forty-six, a chimpanzee has forty-eight, a potato also has forty-eight and a dog has seventy-eight, so the number plainly says nothing about how clever or complex a creature is.
