What counts is what the genes say, and not how the DNA happens to be divided up into bundles.

The DNA of a human and a chimpanzee is more than ninety-eight per cent the same, a reminder of how recently the two lines separated by the standards of evolution. Even fruit flies and baker's yeast carry genes that are clearly related to ours, and scientists can sometimes swap a human gene into yeast and find that it does its old job. Such discoveries are among the strongest evidence that all living things share a common ancestry.

Fruit flies were Amara's favourite creatures, and she explained that they breed in about ten days, cost almost nothing to keep and fit by the hundred into a single milk bottle. Around 1910 an American scientist named Thomas Hunt Morgan noticed a white-eyed male among thousands of ordinary red-eyed flies, and by following its descendants he showed that genes are carried on chromosomes. Laboratories have used the little flies ever since to uncover how genes shape bodies, brains and behaviour.

Neanderthals were not the dim brutes of old cartoons, Amara said, but a closely related kind of human who lived in Europe and western Asia for hundreds of thousands of years. They made tools, controlled fire, hunted large animals, cared for people who were injured, and they vanished from the record around forty thousand years ago, not long after modern humans arrived in their lands. For decades nobody knew what had happened to them, and DNA has given a surprising partial answer.

Remarkably, scientists can now read DNA taken from bones that are tens of thousands of years old, and the results have rewritten some chapters of human history. They show that our ancestors met and had children with Neanderthals, so that people whose roots lie outside Africa today carry about one or two per cent Neanderthal DNA. Some of those inherited genes appear to influence things such as skin, immunity and how the body copes with the environment.

In 2010 scientists announced that DNA from a single finger bone, found in a cave in Siberia, belonged to a previously unknown group of humans whom they named the Denisovans. People in parts of Asia and Oceania today carry a small share of Denisovan DNA, and the version of the gene that helps Tibetan highlanders cope with thin air seems to have come from them. Noor suddenly remembered the mountain people from earlier in the summer, and thought that the story of our species was becoming more tangled and more wonderful by the day.

The story of DNA, Amara told Noor, began long before anyone thought of a double helix, in 1869, when a young Swiss scientist named Friedrich Miescher collected cells from used hospital bandages and studied them under a microscope. Inside their nuclei he found a pale, unfamiliar substance rich in phosphorus, which he named nuclein and which we now call DNA. He had no idea of its importance, and for the best part of eighty years most scientists doubted that such a plain-looking chemical could carry the secrets of heredity.

For decades most scientists assumed that proteins, which are varied and complex, must be the carriers of heredity, and that DNA was merely a dull scaffold. In 1944 a team led by Oswald Avery showed in a careful series of experiments on bacteria that a harmless strain could be changed into a dangerous one simply by giving it DNA from the dangerous one. Further experiments in 1952 supported the finding, and by the early 1950s it was clear that DNA was the molecule of heredity.

Around 1950 a biochemist named Erwin Chargaff measured the four letters in DNA taken from many different living things, and noticed a remarkable regularity. Whatever the species, the amount of A was always very close to the amount of T, and the amount of C was always very close to the amount of G, although the proportions varied between species. It was a vital clue, although at that time nobody could see what it was a clue to.

By the early 1950s the shape of DNA had become one of the great unsolved puzzles of science, and several teams were racing to find it. In Cambridge, two young men named Francis Crick and James Watson were building models and thinking, while in London, Maurice Wilkins and Rosalind Franklin were taking X-ray pictures of DNA at King's College. Another scientist in America, Linus Pauling, was working on it too, and the prize was open to anyone who was clever, careful and a little lucky.

Rosalind Franklin was a brilliant scientist who had trained in chemistry and become one of the best experts in the world in using X-rays to study tiny structures. She and her student Raymond Gosling prepared thin fibres of DNA, shone narrow beams of X-rays through them, and recorded the patterns that the beams made on film, and she measured those patterns with a precision that few could match. Amara said that Franklin was the sort of scientist who would not announce a result until she was quite sure of it.

One of the images that Franklin and Gosling produced in 1952, which is now known as Photo 51, shows a dark X-shaped cross of spots and smudges on a pale ground. To an expert, that pattern could only come from a helix, and the distances between the spots told her how wide the spiral was and how far apart its turns lay. Noor looked at the faded picture in Amara's book and thought it was strange that something so plain could unlock so much.

In 1953, Francis Crick and James Watson announced that DNA is a double helix, building a model from metal plates and wire to show how it fits together. They relied heavily on the X-ray photographs taken in London by Rosalind Franklin, whose careful work revealed the spiral pattern and which they saw without her full knowledge. Watson, Crick and Maurice Wilkins shared the Nobel Prize in 1962, four years after Franklin had died, and her contribution is now widely and rightly honoured.

The report that Watson and Crick sent to the journal Nature, which appeared in April 1953, was barely a page long and included a small drawing of the double helix. Near the end they added one of the most famous understatements in science, remarking that the pairing they had suggested pointed straight to a possible way of copying the genetic material. Noor remembered the unzipping ladder that Amara had drawn, and realised that the shape of DNA and the way it is copied were really two halves of the same idea.

After the work on DNA, Franklin moved to another college in London and studied the structure of viruses with great success, and then in 1958 she died of cancer at the young age of thirty-seven. For many years the part she played was underestimated, but historians and scientists have since set the record straight, and now research awards, university buildings and even a planned space rover for Mars carry her name. Science, Amara said, is a team effort, and fairness in giving credit is part of doing it well.

That afternoon Noor built her own model of DNA from two lengths of wire and a shoebox of coloured beads, using red and blue to stand for A and T and green and yellow for C and G. When the last rung was in place, she twisted the whole thing slowly into a spiral, and it stood on the garden table like a tiny glittering ladder. Idris declared that it was better than any science exhibit, and asked if it could be hung from his bedroom ceiling.

On Monday Amara took Noor to the laboratory where she worked, a long bright room full of benches, humming fridges and machines with blinking lights. Noor was given a white coat three sizes too big and a pair of safety glasses, and she promised faithfully that she would touch nothing unless she was asked. Dr Okafor, who worked at the next bench, shook her hand very seriously and said that she was delighted to meet a new colleague.

In the corner stood a machine the size of a small oven, which Amara called a sequencer and which reads the order of the letters in a piece of DNA. Each letter is marked with a chemical tag that glows a different colour, and a camera records the flashes one after another, turning a long glowing sequence into a string of As, Cs, Gs and Ts on the computer screen. Noor watched the colours scroll past and felt as though she were reading over the shoulder of life itself.

No machine can read an entire genome in a single sweep, Amara said, so the DNA is chopped into millions of short fragments, and each one is read separately. A computer then searches for places where the ends of two fragments overlap and slowly joins them up, rather like reassembling a book that has been torn into scraps by finding the pages whose edges match. It is a vast jigsaw puzzle, and the processors that solve it are among the busiest in the building.

The idea of reading the whole human genome seemed almost absurd when it was proposed in the 1980s, but in 1990 the Human Genome Project began, with teams in six countries sharing the work. Their goal was to read all three billion letters of human DNA, and to make the results freely available to everyone, a decision that Amara thought was one of the finest in the history of science. It was a task on the scale of building a great cathedral, and it required a similar mixture of patience and cooperation.

In the year 2000 the teams announced a working draft of the human genome, and the news was celebrated around the world. By 2003 the project was declared essentially complete, two years ahead of schedule, with the sequence covering nearly all of the parts of the genome that the methods of the time could read. It was a bit like reaching the top of a very tall mountain only to find that the view showed even more mountains beyond.

The first reading of the human genome cost billions of dollars and took more than a decade, but the technology has improved faster than almost anything in modern science. Today a laboratory can read an entire human genome in a matter of days for less than a thousand dollars, and hundreds of thousands of people have already had theirs sequenced. Amara said that this change was like going from one handwritten manuscript to a printing press, and that its consequences were still unfolding.

Before the sequence was read, many scientists had guessed that humans would need a hundred thousand genes or more, because people seemed so much more complicated than other animals. The real number of protein-making genes turned out to be only about twenty thousand, which is not so many more than a small laboratory worm possesses, and it taught everyone a lesson about the limits of guessing. Complexity, it seems, comes less from the number of genes than from how cleverly they are used.

It surprised researchers to discover that only about one or two letters in every hundred belong to genes that make proteins, which left the rest of the genome looking like an empty library. Some people called it junk, but we now know that a great deal of it contains switches, signals and other regions that control when and where genes are used. Scientists still argue about exactly how much of it matters, so that this remains an open and exciting question.

Amara told Noor that nearly half of the human genome is made up of repeating pieces called transposons, or jumping genes, which can copy themselves and paste the copies into new places. Among those repeating pieces are the remains of viruses that infected our distant ancestors, and a few of their genes have since been put to use by the body, for example in building the placenta. Not everything in the genome is a useful gene, and not everything that is not a gene is useless, so the picture is subtle.

The humble truth, Amara said, is that the first reading of the human genome had holes in it, regions that were too repetitive for the machines of the day to put in the right order. In 2022 scientists announced a complete sequence of every chromosome from end to end, and now they are reading the genomes of many people from around the world. Noor thought that it was exactly as it should be, since there will soon be no single genome that stands for all of us.

Nearly every cell in your body holds the same set of genes, yet a nerve cell, a skin cell and a liver cell look and behave in entirely different ways. The difference lies in which genes are switched on, because each type of cell uses only the part of the instruction book that it needs and keeps the rest closed. This careful control is how one fertilised egg grows into hundreds of kinds of cell, all working together in a single body.

Next to many genes, Amara explained, there are stretches of DNA that make no protein at all but work like switches, and special proteins attach to them to turn a gene on, off, or up and down like a dimmer. A skin cell and a liver cell contain exactly the same genes, but each has a different set of switches pressed, which is why the two look and behave so differently. Reading a genome, she said, is a bit like reading a score and knowing which players are on stage.

Every person begins as a single fertilised egg, Amara said, which divides into two, then four, then eight, and so on until there is a ball of cells that are still unspecialised and known as stem cells. As the embryo grows, these cells are steered into different roles, each one switching on its own pattern of genes and settling into the identity of a nerve, a muscle or a skin cell. A human body ends up with around two hundred distinct kinds of cell, all produced from a single set of instructions.

A special family of master genes, known as the Hox genes, acts like a team of site managers in the growing embryo, telling each region of the body what it is supposed to become. They decide where the head goes, where the chest goes and where the limbs grow, and a mistake in one of them can put a leg in a fly where an antenna ought to be. Remarkably, humans carry related versions of the same genes, which sit in the same order along the chromosomes, and this is another sign of our distant kinship with flies.

Amara described a layer of control that sits on top of the DNA itself, in the form of small chemical tags that can switch genes on or off without altering a single letter. This field is called epigenetics, and it shows that diet, stress and age can leave marks on the way genes behave. How much of this is passed down to children in humans, however, is still debated, and scientists are careful not to promise more than the evidence supports.

Grandma's calico cat, Biscuit, was asleep on the garden wall, and Amara used her coat to explain how tags can silence a whole chromosome. In a female mammal each cell randomly switches off one of its two X chromosomes early in development, and the pattern is then copied into all of that cell's descendants. If one X carries an orange version of the colour gene and the other a black version, the result is a patchwork of orange and black, which is why nearly every calico cat is female.

Identical twins, Amara said, offer one of the clearest demonstrations that the tags on DNA change with life. Studies have found that young twins have very similar patterns of chemical tags, but that older twins, particularly those who have lived in different places or had different habits, show more and more differences between their patterns. Their letters are still the same, so it is the layer above, the one that switches genes on and off, that records the difference in their lives.

One famous study concerns the Dutch Hunger Winter of 1944 and 1945, when a blockade left much of the western Netherlands desperately short of food. Researchers have since followed the people who were still unborn at that time, and they found that decades later such people had slightly higher rates of some health problems and small differences in the tags on some genes. The findings suggest that conditions before birth can leave lasting marks, though scientists are careful to point out that the study cannot prove every detail of how.

In the beehive at the end of Grandma's garden, Amara pointed out the larger queen moving slowly among a crowd of smaller workers and said that they had the same genes. A grub that is fed a special food called royal jelly develops into a queen, who is bigger, lays thousands of eggs and lives for years, whereas the others become workers and live for weeks. It is a vivid example of how the same recipe book can produce two quite different creatures, according to which pages are used.

Amara ended the day with a note of caution, because popular books and websites sometimes claim that the experiences of one generation can be written into the genes of the next. Scientists agree that chemical tags matter for how genes are used, yet most tags are wiped clean when eggs and sperm are made, so the evidence for inheriting them in people remains thin. It is an exciting question, she said, and good scientists will keep asking it without promising an answer before it is found.

Amara drew a cell and filled it with little bean-shaped objects, which she called mitochondria, the power plants of the cell. They take the sugars from your food and the oxygen from your breath and turn them into a chemical that cells can spend as energy, and a hard-working muscle cell may carry thousands of them. Noor thought that it was the most important thing she had heard so far, since she was always hungry, and without mitochondria she would not be able to run.

Mitochondria, Amara went on, have a remarkable history, for most scientists believe that they began as free-living bacteria. More than a billion years ago a larger cell swallowed one of them and, instead of digesting it, struck up a partnership in which the bacterium made energy and the larger cell gave it protection and food. That is why mitochondria still carry a little DNA of their own, shaped in a small circle like the DNA of bacteria.

Besides the DNA in the nucleus, each cell holds a little more inside its mitochondria, the tiny power plants that turn food into usable energy. This mitochondrial DNA is inherited almost always from the mother, because the egg supplies these parts to the embryo while the sperm contributes very few. Scientists use it to trace maternal lines far back in time, since it changes only slowly from one generation to the next.

Noor drew a line from herself to Mum, from Mum to Grandma and from Grandma to Grandma's mother, and Amara pointed out that this was the path travelled by her mitochondrial DNA. Idris carried the same kind, as it came from Mum as well, but he could not pass it on, and in this branch of the family it would stop with him. Noor had the odd feeling of looking at a thread that ran backwards through hundreds of generations of women, unbroken.

Scientists who compare the mitochondrial DNA of people around the world find that every line leads back, eventually, to one woman who lived in Africa roughly one hundred and fifty to two hundred thousand years ago. She is sometimes called Mitochondrial Eve, though this name is rather misleading, because she was neither the first woman nor the only one alive at the time, and our other ancestors from that period have left plenty of other DNA. She is simply the point where one particular thread of inheritance happens to meet.

Mitochondrial DNA is passed along the female line, Amara said, and there is a counterpart on the male side in the Y chromosome, which passes from a father to his sons and changes only slowly. In many cultures a surname travels in the same direction, so the two sometimes match, and scientists have used Y chromosomes to test whether men with the same surname are related. The match is imperfect, however, since adoption, name changes and unrecorded secrets have a way of blurring the picture.

In 2012 archaeologists digging beneath a car park in Leicester found a skeleton that they suspected to be King Richard the Third, who had died in battle more than five hundred years earlier. Because mitochondrial DNA passes along the female line, the scientists were able to compare it with that of living descendants of the king's sister, and the match, combined with other evidence, convinced experts that the bones were his. Noor was thrilled that a thread of DNA could reach through five centuries to name a king.

Noor unrolled a long strip of paper and drew her ancestors row by row, finding that the numbers doubled each time, from two parents to four grandparents and eight great-grandparents, and on to sixteen and thirty-two. If she kept going for thirty generations, about eight hundred years, there would be more than a billion places in the tree, which is far more people than lived on Earth at that time. The answer, Amara said, is that the same ancestors fill many places, so that everyone alive is related to everyone else through countless overlapping lines.

There was one more twist that Amara thought Noor would enjoy, which is that you do not inherit equal amounts of DNA from every ancestor. The pieces that arrive from each of them get smaller and fewer with every generation, so after perhaps ten generations a person may carry no DNA at all from some ancestors who are in her family tree. Family history and DNA history, she concluded, are close cousins rather than twins, and each can fill gaps that the other leaves.

That evening Grandma sat in her favourite armchair and told the story of her own grandmother, who had sailed across the sea as a young woman with one suitcase and a sewing machine. Noor listened with her notebook closed, because for once she did not feel that she needed to write anything down, and Amara said afterwards that stories and DNA are two different ways in which a family remembers its past. Each can be lost, and each can surprise you, and the best family histories use both.

A small number of illnesses, Amara said, are caused by a change in one single gene, and the pattern is rather like Mendel's peas. Cystic fibrosis, which affects the lungs and digestion, appears only when a child inherits a changed copy from both parents, each of whom is usually a healthy carrier with no idea of it. For conditions like this, the rules of inheritance allow doctors to estimate the chance that a family will be affected.

The gene involved in cystic fibrosis, Amara explained, is called CFTR, and it makes a protein that works like a small gate in the wall of a cell, letting salt and water pass through. When the gate is faulty, the mucus that lines the lungs and the digestive system becomes thick and sticky instead of thin and slippery, which makes infections more likely and food harder to digest. It is a good example of how a tiny mistake in one gene can lead, through one protein, to a whole pattern of symptoms.

Most people with a changed copy of the CFTR gene are not ill at all, Amara said, because the working copy makes enough of the protein to do the job. Such a person is called a carrier, and in some populations, for example those of northern European ancestry, about one person in twenty-five is a carrier of this particular change without ever knowing it. Everybody carries a few gene changes of this sort, and most of them never matter, unless two carriers happen to have a child together.

Noor tossed her coins once more while Amara showed her how the rule works for two carrier parents. Each child gets one copy from each parent, so there is a one in four chance of two changed copies, a two in four chance of one of each and a one in four chance of two working ones. The odds are the same for every child, just as a coin cannot remember how the previous toss landed, and this is exactly the arithmetic that Mendel worked out with his peas.

Dr Okafor, who joined them for lunch, explained that people with cystic fibrosis follow a daily routine of breathing exercises, physiotherapy and medicines, and that care has improved enormously over the years. Since about 2012 a newer kind of medicine that helps the faulty protein do its job has made a real difference for many patients, though the treatments do not suit everybody and they remain very costly. A diagnosis today, she said, is a very different thing from what it was when her teachers were young.

The most famous family tree in the history of genetics, Amara said, belonged to Queen Victoria of Britain, who carried a change in a gene on the X chromosome that causes haemophilia, in which blood clots very slowly. Her daughters passed it on to royal families in Spain, Germany and Russia, where the heir to the throne suffered from it, and the pattern helped doctors to see how X-linked conditions behave. Boys are affected more often than girls, because a boy has only one X chromosome and no second copy to cover for it.

Not every condition needs two changed copies, Amara said, for in a dominant condition a single changed copy is enough to have an effect. Achondroplasia, a common cause of short stature that is linked to a change in one gene, is an example, and a child of a person who has it has a one in two chance of inheriting it. People with achondroplasia live full and active lives, she added, and doctors are keen to remind everyone that a gene is part of a person and never the whole of them.

Noor was surprised to learn that around four in five children with achondroplasia are born to parents who do not have the condition, and Amara linked this to what they had learned about mutations earlier in the summer. In such cases the gene change arises newly in an egg or a sperm cell, so that nothing in the family history could have predicted it, and nobody has done anything to cause it. New mutations can appear in any family, she said, and there is never anything to blame.

Cystic fibrosis and haemophilia are among the better-known genetic conditions, Amara said, yet doctors know of thousands of rarer ones, and many of them are caused by changes in a single gene. Each is uncommon, but added together they affect many families, and reading a patient's genome can now give an answer in cases where the cause was a mystery for years. For a family that has waited a long time to understand what is wrong, an answer can be a relief, even when no treatment exists.

That evening Noor sorted what she had learned onto sticky notes and stuck them in two piles on the garden table, with the conditions that depend mainly on one gene in the smaller pile. Most of the illnesses that affect people, she realised, belong to a different story involving many genes and a lifetime of influences, and that story was the next thing Amara had promised to explain. She wrote one more note and put it on top, which said that nobody is ever defined by a condition.

Most of the illnesses that affect large numbers of people, such as heart disease and type two diabetes, are not caused by any single gene. Hundreds or even thousands of small genetic differences each add a tiny amount to a person's risk, and food, exercise, smoking and many other factors push the risk up or down. That is why a family history is a useful warning but never a sentence, and why healthy habits help people whatever genes they hold.

How do scientists find the small genetic differences that matter for common illnesses, Noor asked, and Amara described studies in which the DNA of tens of thousands, and sometimes millions, of people is compared. Researchers look for letters that turn up more often in people with a condition than in people without it, and each is a signpost pointing to a region of the genome that deserves a closer look. The signposts do not give an explanation in themselves, but they have led to many discoveries about how illnesses begin.

The surprising finding of such studies, Amara said, is that each of the many gene differences linked to a common illness changes the chance of getting it by only a tiny amount. Taken alone, a difference might raise the risk by a few per cent, far too little to say anything about one person, so it is the combination of many of them, along with life, that matters. She asked Noor to imagine a huge crowd each giving a very gentle push, with no one pushing hard enough to be blamed.

Scientists can add up the effects of thousands of small differences into a single figure called a polygenic score, which roughly shows whether a person's inherited chance of a condition is above or below average. It is a modest tool and not a crystal ball, Amara said, and it tends to work best for the groups of people who were included most often in the original studies, which has raised important questions of fairness. Researchers are working to include many more people from around the world to fix that imbalance.

The oldest and cheapest genetic test of all, Amara said with a smile, is the question that doctors have always asked about illnesses in your family. A pattern of a condition among close relatives can be a valuable clue to an inherited chance, though families also share meals, habits and homes, so it does not prove that genes are the cause. That is why a doctor's skill lies in weighing all the clues together and not just one of them.

Phenylketonuria is a rare condition in which a changed gene leaves the body unable to break down an amino acid found in many protein-rich foods, and without treatment it can seriously harm a child's brain. Because newborns in many countries are screened with a tiny drop of blood from the heel, the condition is usually discovered within days, and a carefully planned diet then lets the child grow up healthy. It is a striking example of how knowing a gene and changing the environment can work together.

In one large study, researchers looked at people who carried a higher inherited chance of heart disease and compared those who kept healthy habits with those who did not. The people who ate sensibly, stayed active and avoided smoking had a much lower chance of a heart attack than the others, which showed that genetic risk can be offset, at least partly, by how a person lives. Amara said that it was one of the most cheering results in modern genetics, because it put some power back into people's hands.

A small number of gene changes do have a large effect on the risk of common illnesses, Amara said, and one well-known example is a group of changes in two genes called BRCA1 and BRCA2. People who inherit certain changes in these genes have a much higher than average chance of some kinds of cancer, though it is not a certainty, and many carriers never develop it. Knowing about such a change can allow a person and a doctor to plan extra check-ups or other steps, which is why some families choose to be tested.

Genetic tests can reveal that a person carries a changed gene, or has a higher or lower chance of developing a particular condition, but they rarely deliver a definite verdict. For this reason, genetic counsellors are trained to explain what a result means, what it does not mean, and what choices follow from it. Amara stressed that the information belongs to the person tested, and that nobody should be pressured to learn more about their own DNA than they wish to know.

Dr Okafor invited Noor into her small quiet office, with its comfortable chairs and its box of tissues, and described what a genetic counsellor does all day. She listens carefully, explains what a test can and cannot show, and helps people think through what they would do with the answer, but she never tells anyone what to choose. Noor asked whether she herself would want to know, and Dr Okafor smiled and said that people honestly answer that question in different ways, and that nobody should ever be rushed to find out.

Noor had seen advertisements for kits that promise to reveal where your family came from, and she asked how they work. The companies compare your DNA with reference samples from people in different regions, and then estimate which of those groups you resemble most closely. The answers are probabilities rather than facts, and they can shift as the databases improve, so a result should be treated as an interesting clue instead of a definite verdict.

Amara told Noor that these kits do not usually read the whole genome but test several hundred thousand chosen spots where people are known to differ. The pattern is then compared with patterns from groups of people whose families have lived for a long time in particular parts of the world, and a computer calculates which of those groups the sample most resembles. The whole exercise is only as good as the database behind it, and databases are bigger for some parts of the world than for others.

Amara added that two companies can give the same person two different answers, because each uses its own database and its own methods, and the results are really estimates with a margin of error. Even full brothers and sisters can receive quite different percentages, since each inherits a different shuffle of the family's DNA, and a region on the map is a place where certain gene versions are common and not a nationality. Noor decided that the best way to read such results was with a pinch of salt.

One of the most useful things such tests can do, Amara said, is to find relatives, because two people who share long matching stretches of DNA must have a recent common ancestor. Some people who were adopted as children have found their birth families this way, and distant cousins have discovered each other across continents. The same technology also raises delicate questions, for a test can reveal secrets that nobody expected, such as a father who is not the one the family believed.

In 1984, a British scientist realised that certain stretches of DNA differ so much between people that they can be used like a fingerprint. The method has since been used to identify criminals, to free people who were wrongly convicted, and to settle questions about who is related to whom. Except for identical twins, no two people share the same pattern, which is why even a tiny sample, such as a single hair root, can be so valuable.

The method relies on stretches of DNA in which a short pattern of letters is repeated over and over, and people differ in how many repeats they carry at each of these places. Laboratories check about twenty such spots, and although any one of them might match by chance between two people, the chance that all twenty would match between two unrelated people is smaller than one in many billions. This is why a profile can work as a reliable identifier, provided that the sample is handled with great care.

The new method made its debut in a criminal case in England in 1986, where it proved that a young man who had confessed to a serious crime was innocent and then helped police to find the real culprit. Since then DNA evidence has helped to convict guilty people and to free innocent ones who had spent years in prison, and it is also used in the simpler task of showing whether a man is a child's father. Amara said that few scientific discoveries have changed the way courtrooms work so much, and so quickly, in a single generation.

Noor wondered who owns a person's DNA, and Amara replied that this is one of the hardest questions of the age. Your genome is intensely personal, but it also says something about your parents, brothers, sisters and cousins, who never agreed to be tested, so rules are needed about who may store it, see it and use it. Many countries have laws to prevent misuse, and the debate over where to draw the lines continues.

Like any other evidence, Amara said, DNA has its limits, and the first of them is that finding someone's DNA at a place shows that it was there, but not how it got there or when. A cup might carry a visitor's DNA from a perfectly innocent visit, and samples can be mixed, contaminated or too small to be sure about, so a careful scientist reports what the evidence can support and nothing more. It remains among the strongest tools available to investigators, but it is never a magic answer.

Grandma, who had been listening with interest, decided to try one of the kits herself, and a few weeks later an email arrived with the results. Most of them matched the places mentioned in her family stories, but a small percentage pointed to a region she had never heard of, which led to much debate at the kitchen table about who might have been where. Amara reminded everyone that the figures were estimates, and Grandma declared that she was going to treat the surprise as an invitation to find out more.

On a hot Thursday Noor's friend Jun came round to the garden with a football under his arm and a question that he had clearly been saving up. His cousin was brilliant at maths, he said, and he wanted to know whether people were simply born clever, or whether it was something you could build, like muscles. Amara put down her coffee, pulled up a chair and said that it was exactly the kind of question that deserved a proper answer.

The brain, Amara began, is made of tens of billions of nerve cells, and thousands of genes help to build them, wire them together and keep them working. Yet the genes only set up the basic framework, because the connections between the cells are strengthened or weakened by everything a child sees, hears, learns and practises, so the finished brain is the work of genes and experience together. A brain without any experience would be like an orchestra that had never played a note.

Studies of large groups of people have found thousands of tiny gene differences that are linked, very slightly, to scores in tests of thinking skills. Each of these has a minuscule effect, and even all of them together explain only part of the differences between people in a group, which means that they are of little use in predicting what any single person can do. Amara added that such tests measure only certain kinds of skill, and that there are many ways of being clever.

Surroundings matter enormously, Amara went on, and she listed good schools, nourishing food, plenty of sleep, books in the home and adults who talk to children. Average scores on tests of thinking skills rose steadily in many countries through the twentieth century, far too quickly for the genes of whole populations to have changed, which suggests that the environment can make a very large difference. Genes may influence how easily a child learns, but nobody learns without something to learn from.

Personality works in much the same way, Amara said, and studies of twins suggest that genes account for roughly a third to a half of the differences between people in traits such as shyness, curiosity and sociability. That leaves at least half to be explained by family, friends, school, culture and the countless accidents of life, and a shy child can learn to speak up while a bold one may grow quiet. A trait that is partly inherited is not, for that reason, a trait that is fixed.

Every morning that week Noor sat at Grandma's old piano and worked through her scales and a short tune while a metronome ticked beside her. She noticed that the tune sounded a little better each day, and she realised that she was watching a lesson in genetics at close range, since skill grows with practice and nobody gets it for free. Grandma, who had been taught the piano as a girl, said that it was exactly how she remembered learning.

There is a subtle twist, Amara said, which is that genes and surroundings do not simply add together but affect one another all the time. A child with a slight leaning towards reading will tend to pick up books, spend more time on them and become a better reader, and that practice shapes the brain further, so a small nudge grows into a larger difference. Jun listened closely, and said that this was exactly what had happened with his football.

Amara mentioned one more kind of study, which follows identical twins who were separated when they were young and brought up in different homes. Some of these pairs, when they met as adults, turned out to be alike in surprising ways, in their tastes, their habits and even their manner of speaking, and the studies suggested that genes can reach further than anyone expected. Other scientists warn that the twins sometimes had more in common in their upbringing than it first seemed, so the evidence should be read with some care.

Noor asked whether this meant that her whole life was already written in her genes, and Amara answered with a firm and cheerful no. Genes shape what is possible and make some outcomes a little more likely than others, but they work through a lifetime of experiences, choices and pieces of luck that nobody can fully predict. She told Noor to think of her DNA as a starting point rather than a script.

Before Jun went home, Noor tore a page from her Question Book and wrote out a list of everything that genes cannot decide for you, and she handed it to him with a flourish. It included how hard you practise, what you choose to learn, who you decide to be kind to and what you do on the day after a failure, which were precisely the things that mattered most. Jun folded the page carefully, put it into his pocket and said that he would keep it, in case his cousin ever tried to boast again.

If a gene is faulty or missing, Amara asked Noor, what is the most obvious thing a doctor could try to do about it? The answer was to give the patient's cells a working copy, which is the idea behind gene therapy, and it is simple to state but extraordinarily difficult to carry out. The copy has to reach the right cells, it has to be used at the right level, and it has to be safe, and each of those problems took scientists decades to solve.

Viruses, Amara said, are extremely good at one thing, which is getting their genes inside cells, and scientists decided to borrow that talent. They take a virus, remove the genes that make it harmful, and load the empty shell with a working copy of the gene that a patient needs, so that it can carry the cargo to the right cells. Noor thought that it was a splendid example of turning an enemy's best trick against itself.

The early years of gene therapy were not a story of easy success, Amara told Noor honestly. In 1999 a young volunteer in an American trial died after a reaction to the treatment, and in a few other trials patients developed serious problems, which made scientists and regulators stop and think very hard. The field became far more careful about safety and honesty as a result, and the lessons learned in those difficult years laid the ground for the progress that followed.

Since those hard early years, Amara said, careful work has produced treatments that are now approved for use in a few rare inherited conditions. A therapy for one form of inherited blindness was approved in the United States in 2017, and another for a serious muscle-wasting illness called spinal muscular atrophy followed in 2019, and in a number of cases the results have been remarkable. These are not cures for every patient, but they show that the idea can work.

The story of CRISPR, Amara said, began quietly in 1987, when scientists noticed strange repeating patterns in the DNA of bacteria and wondered what on earth they were for. For many years the patterns were a mystery, until in 2007 researchers working with yoghurt bacteria showed that they act as a defence system, in which the bacteria keep snippets of virus DNA like a gallery of mugshots. When the same virus attacks again, the bacteria recognise it at once and cut up its DNA.

In 2012 two scientists working in different countries showed that the bacterial defence system could be turned into a tool for editing any DNA, and they were awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it in 2020. A short guide molecule made of RNA is designed to match one chosen spot in the DNA, and it leads a protein called Cas9 there, like a pair of scissors guided by a map, and the protein makes a cut. Once the DNA is cut, the cell tries to repair it, and scientists can use that repair to switch off a gene or to put in a new piece.

Amara compared CRISPR to the find and replace tool in a word processor, which searches a huge document for a particular phrase and changes it, though with the difference that this document has three billion letters. The tool can occasionally cut at a place that looks similar but is not the right one, so scientists check carefully, and newer versions called base editors can change a single letter without cutting both strands. Precision, she said, is the most important word in the whole business, and the people who work with it never forget that.

In 2023, regulators in Britain and the United States approved the first medicine based on CRISPR, and it was designed to treat sickle cell disease. Doctors take blood-forming cells from the patient, edit them in the laboratory, and return them to the body, where they make healthier red blood cells. The treatment is complex and costly, and its long-term results are still being followed, but it marked a historic turning point.

The same tools can be used on plants, Amara said, and researchers have already edited tomatoes, mushrooms and many crops to resist disease, to last longer or to grow in tougher conditions. Farmers have been changing plants for thousands of years by choosing which seeds to sow, and Mendel's peas were part of that long tradition, so editing can be seen as a faster way of doing something old. Countries have different rules about it, and people disagree about whether and how it should be used, which is exactly why those debates matter.

Noor put down her pencil and asked whether all of these treatments would be available to everyone who needed them, and Amara admitted that it is one of the hardest questions of all. Some gene therapies cost more than a million dollars for a single patient, and many of the people who could benefit, including those with sickle cell disease in Africa and India, live where such treatment is almost impossible to reach. Medical science has little value, she said, if only a small number of the world's people are able to use it.

Editing a patient's blood cells affects only that patient, but changing the DNA of an embryo would alter every cell and be passed to all of that person's descendants. For that reason, scientists and governments have raised hard questions about safety, fairness and consent, and most countries do not allow edited embryos to be used to start a pregnancy. Amara said that these decisions belong to society as a whole, and not to scientists alone.

In 2018 a scientist in China surprised the world by announcing that he had used CRISPR on human embryos and that babies had been born from them. The reaction was swift and almost entirely negative, for scientists everywhere said that the work was premature, unsafe and carried out without proper oversight, and a Chinese court later sent him to prison. Since then, many countries have made it clear in law or in guidance that editing embryos to start a pregnancy is not allowed.

Noor asked whether people would one day design their babies, and Amara explained that there is a big difference between preventing a serious inherited illness and trying to choose talents or looks. Since most traits depend on thousands of genes and on a lifetime of experience, nobody can currently order a particular height or personality, and many experts doubt that it will ever be possible. There are still hard questions about where to draw the line, she added, and they should be decided by everyone and not only by scientists.

In 1883 an English scholar named Francis Galton, a relative of Charles Darwin, coined the word eugenics for the idea that the human race could be improved by encouraging some people to have children and discouraging others. It sounded scientific and modern to many educated people, and it spread to Europe and America in the early twentieth century, even though its authors knew almost nothing about how traits are truly inherited. Amara asked Noor to remember this story carefully, because it showed how dangerous a bad idea can be when it is dressed up as science.

In the early twentieth century, a movement called eugenics claimed that society could be improved by deciding who should and should not have children. Its supporters used poor science and plain prejudice, and it led to great suffering, including forced sterilisation in many countries and, under the Nazis in Germany, far worse. Amara said that this history is a lasting warning that genes must never be used to rank people or to judge anyone's worth.

Eugenics was wrong in two separate ways, Amara said, and both of them still matter today. The science was poor, because most traits depend on many genes and on the environment, so nobody can sort people into good and bad by their DNA. The morality was worse, because no person or government has the right to decide that someone else's life is worth less, and genetics is at its best when it helps people, with their consent, as equals.

To finish her project, Noor drew a family tree that stretched back to her great-grandparents and marked who had curls, who had green eyes and who had freckles. She could see traits appearing in one generation, skipping the next and then returning, just as the pea plants had shown more than a century and a half earlier. The tree no longer looked like a puzzle to her, but like a story told in many small pieces.

On the last page of her Question Book, Noor wrote a heading that said still unknown, and underneath it she listed all of the things that nobody has yet worked out. How exactly do thousands of tiny differences add up to a personality, she wondered, and how much of the genome is truly useful, and what other secrets are hidden in old bones? Amara read the list with pleasure and said that science is mostly a careful way of finding out what we do not know, and that it was the best part.

Amara said that people often call the genome a blueprint, but she preferred to think of it as a book of recipes. A blueprint fixes every detail in advance, whereas a recipe can turn out differently depending on the ingredients, the oven, the cook and the day. In the same way, a body is the result of genes being read and used in a particular environment, which is why no two people ever end up exactly alike.

By the end of the summer, Noor understood that her curls and her green eyes were gifts from many generations, shuffled together in a way that would never be repeated. She understood too that her genes were only the beginning of the story, because what she learned, chose and did would shape her just as surely. Remember that this book offers general information about genetics, and it is not medical advice, so anyone with questions about their own health should speak to a doctor or a genetic counsellor.
